00Orientation

The big map: what is system design?

System design is deciding the parts of a software system and how they talk to each other so that it stays fast, correct and cheap as it grows.

At Ramu's chai stall

Ramu sells tea from a single cart near Medinipur station. He boils the water, takes the money and remembers who wants less sugar. For 50 customers a day, that's perfect.

Then a food blogger posts about his elaichi chai. Next morning, 2,000 people turn up. The kettle is too small, the queue blocks the road, he forgets orders, and the cash box overflows. Nothing about his tea changed. His system broke because the load changed. That is exactly the problem system design solves.

System design questions come at two zoom levels. Think of building a city:

High-Level Design (HLD)Low-Level Design (LLD)
Question it answersWhich components exist and how do they connect?Which classes exist and how do they collaborate?
Unit of designServices, databases, caches, queues, load balancersClasses, interfaces, methods, objects
Main worriesScale, availability, latency, consistency, costReadability, extensibility, testability, correctness
Typical outputBox-and-arrow architecture diagram, API list, data model, capacity estimateClass diagram, interfaces, working code
Interview example"Design WhatsApp", "Design a URL shortener""Design a parking lot", "Design an elevator"
Tools of the tradeCaching, sharding, replication, CAP, queuesOOP, SOLID, design patterns, UML

The cast: chai stall ↔ technology

At the chai stallIn a software systemChapter

Each worker doing one job wellSingle Responsibility Principle28

The four questions behind every design

Scalability

Can it handle 10× or 100× more users by adding machines?

Availability

Does it keep working when a machine, a disk or a whole data centre dies?

Performance

How fast is one request (latency), and how many per second can it serve (throughput)?

Maintainability

Can new developers understand and change it without breaking things? This is where LLD and SOLID live.

Lock it in

HLD = the city. LLD = the rooms. SOLID = the building code.

Every design is a trade-off. There is no "best" architecture, only the best one for these requirements. Saying "it depends, and here is what it depends on" is the most senior sentence in system design.

Quick check

What is the difference between HLD and LLD in one sentence each?

HLD describes the major components of a system (services, databases, caches, queues) and how data flows between them. LLD describes the internals of one component: its classes, interfaces, relationships and methods.

Why do systems that work fine on day one break later?

Because load, data size and team size grow. A design that ignores scale, failure and change works only until one of those grows past what a single machine or a single tangled codebase can handle.

01HLD · Foundations

How a request travels

A client asks, a server answers. Everything else in this book is about making that conversation fast, reliable and able to happen millions of times a second.

At Ramu's chai stall

A tourist steps off the train and wants Ramu's famous chai. She doesn't know where the stall is, so she asks the station porter, who knows every shop's location. He says "Platform 2, next to the bookshop." She walks over, says "One elaichi chai, less sugar," pays, and gets her cup.

Map it: the tourist is the client, the porter is DNS (turns a name into an address), the walk is the network, "one elaichi chai" is the request, Ramu is the server, and the cup of tea is the response.

Definition

Client–server model: a client (browser, mobile app, another service) sends a request over the network to a server, which processes it and sends back a response. The server waits for requests; the client starts the conversation.

What happens when you type a URL and press Enter

This is the single most common warm-up question in interviews. Here is the full journey for https://www.ramuchai.in/menu:

  1. DNS lookupThe browser checks its cache, then the OS, then asks a DNS resolver. The resolver walks the hierarchy: root → .in TLD → the domain's authoritative name server, which returns the IP address.
  2. TCP connectionThree-way handshake: client sends SYN, server replies SYN-ACK, client sends ACK. Now there is a reliable pipe.
  3. TLS handshake (for HTTPS)Server proves its identity with a certificate; both sides agree on encryption keys. From now on, everything is encrypted.
  4. HTTP requestThe browser sends GET /menu with headers (cookies, accepted formats, user agent).
  5. Server workA load balancer may forward it to one app server, which runs business logic, hits a cache or database and builds a response.
  6. HTTP responseStatus code, headers and body (HTML or JSON) come back.
  7. RenderingThe browser parses HTML, fetches CSS, JS and images (often from a CDN), and paints the page.

HTTP in two tables

MethodMeaningSafe?Idempotent?Chai example
GETRead a resourceYesYesSee the menu
POSTCreate / trigger an actionNoNoPlace a new order
PUTReplace a resource completelyNoYesReplace the whole order
PATCHChange part of a resourceNoNot guaranteedChange sugar level only
DELETERemove a resourceNoYesCancel the order

Idempotent means doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. Deleting order #42 twice still leaves order #42 deleted. Posting "new order" twice creates two orders. This matters hugely for retries (Chapter 13).

Status familyMeaningOnes to know
2xxSuccess200 OK · 201 Created · 204 No Content
3xxGo somewhere else301 Moved Permanently · 302 Found · 304 Not Modified (use your cache)
4xxYou (client) made a mistake400 Bad Request · 401 Unauthenticated · 403 Forbidden · 404 Not Found · 409 Conflict · 429 Too Many Requests
5xxI (server) made a mistake500 Internal Error · 502 Bad Gateway · 503 Unavailable · 504 Gateway Timeout

TCP vs UDP

TCP: registered post

Connection first, then every packet is numbered, acknowledged and resent if lost. Arrives complete and in order. Used by HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, databases, email.

UDP: shouting across the room

No connection, no guarantee. Some words may be lost, but it's very fast. Used for video calls, online games, DNS queries, and HTTP/3 (QUIC builds reliability on top of UDP).

In plain words

An IP address is a building's street address. A port is the flat number inside it (443 for HTTPS, 3306 for MySQL, 6379 for Redis). DNS is the phone book that turns "ramuchai.in" into the street address. HTTP is the language the visitor and the shopkeeper agree to speak.

Lock it in

"Dina Tried To Have Really Rich Rasgulla"

DNS → TCP → TLS → HTTP request → Response → Render. And remember: HTTP is stateless; each request carries everything the server needs (cookies, tokens) because the server doesn't remember the previous one.

Interview questions

Why is HTTP called stateless, and how do websites remember that I'm logged in?

Each HTTP request is independent; the protocol has no memory of earlier requests. Websites add state on top: after login the server gives you a session ID cookie (pointing at session data stored on the server or in Redis) or a signed token like a JWT. Your browser sends it with every request, so the server can recognise you again.

What's the difference between 401 and 403?

401 Unauthorized really means unauthenticated: "I don't know who you are; log in." 403 Forbidden means "I know who you are, but you're not allowed to do this."

Where can DNS be used for system design, not just name lookup?

DNS can return different IPs to different users: round-robin across servers, the nearest data centre (geo-DNS), or a healthy region during failover. Its weakness is caching: clients may keep an old IP until the TTL expires, so DNS failover is slow compared with a load balancer.

Next: Scaling: up vs out →
02HLD · Foundations

Scaling: bigger machine or more machines?

Scalability is the ability to handle more load by adding resources. You either buy a bigger machine (scale up) or add more machines (scale out).

At Ramu's chai stall

With 2,000 customers a day, Ramu has two choices. Option A: buy a giant 50-litre kettle and a faster stove. Simple, but there's a limit to how big a kettle gets, it's expensive, and if that one stove breaks, nobody gets tea. Option B: open three more identical stalls next to each other, each with an ordinary kettle. More to coordinate, but he can keep adding stalls, and if one breaks the others keep serving.

Option A is vertical scaling. Option B is horizontal scaling.

Vertical (scale up)Horizontal (scale out)
HowMore CPU, RAM, faster disk on the same machineMore machines sharing the work
LimitHard ceiling: the biggest machine money can buyPractically unlimited
FailureSingle point of failureOne machine dies, others continue
ComplexityVery low; no code changesNeeds load balancing, stateless code, distributed data
Cost curveGets expensive fast at the top endRoughly linear with commodity hardware
Good forEarly stage, relational DB primary, quick fixWeb/app tiers, big data, anything that must stay up

The catch: servers must be stateless

Ramu remembers that Priya takes less sugar. When there are four stalls, Priya might go to stall 3 tomorrow, and stall 3 has never met her. If each stall keeps its own memory, customers get inconsistent service.

Latency vs throughput

Latency: how long one trip takes

Time from request to response, in milliseconds. "My chai arrived in 2 minutes."

Throughput: how many per second

Requests (or bytes) handled per unit of time. "The stall serves 600 cups an hour."

Think of a highway: the speed limit is latency, the number of lanes is throughput. Adding lanes (more servers) raises throughput but doesn't make one car faster. Caching and better algorithms reduce latency.

Measure latency with percentiles, not averages. p50 (median) = half the requests are faster than this. p99 = 99% are faster; the slowest 1% are slower. If your p50 is 80 ms but p99 is 4 seconds, 1 in 100 users is having a terrible time, and the average hides it.

Latency numbers every engineer should know

Rough, rounded numbers. The right-hand column stretches time so that one L1 cache read takes 1 second, which makes the differences easy to feel.

OperationReal timeIf L1 cache = 1 second
L1 CPU cache read0.5 ns1 second
Main memory (RAM) read100 ns3 minutes
Read 1 MB sequentially from RAM~3 µs2 hours
SSD random read~16–100 µs9 hours to 2 days
Round trip inside one data centre0.5 ms12 days
HDD disk seek10 ms8 months
Round trip India ↔ US~200 ms12 years
Lock it in

Memory is a minute, disk is a day, the network is a voyage.

RAM is ~1000× faster than SSD; crossing the planet is slower than everything. That is why we cache in memory, avoid chatty network calls, and put data near users. Scale up first when it's cheap; scale out when you need no ceiling and no single point of failure. Scale-out needs stateless servers.

Interview questions

Your single server is at 90% CPU. What do you do?

First find out why (profiling, slow queries, missing cache). Short term, scaling up is the fastest fix. Long term, make the app stateless, put a load balancer in front and scale horizontally, with auto-scaling based on CPU or request rate. Also look at caching hot reads so less work reaches the server at all.

Why are percentiles better than averages for latency?

Latency distributions have long tails. A few very slow requests barely move the average but hurt real users, and in a microservice call chain the slowest dependency decides the total. p95/p99 expose the tail, so SLOs are written in percentiles.

Next: Load balancing →
03HLD · Building blocks

Load balancing

A load balancer sits in front of many servers and decides which one handles each request, so no single server is overloaded and dead servers are skipped.

At Ramu's chai stall

Four stalls now stand side by side, but everybody crowds stall 1 because it's nearest the station exit. Ramu hires his cousin Bablu to stand at the entrance and point: "You, stall 2. You, stall 3." Bablu also notices when stall 4's stove goes out and stops sending people there until it's fixed.

Bablu is the load balancer. Pointing people in turn is an algorithm. Checking the stoves is a health check.

What a load balancer gives you

Spreads load

No server is idle while another melts.

Hides failures

Health checks pull dead servers out of rotation.

Zero-downtime deploys

Drain one server, update it, put it back, repeat.

One front door

TLS termination, a single domain, easy to add servers behind it.

Layer 4 vs Layer 7

Layer 4 (transport)Layer 7 (application)
Looks atIP address and port onlyFull HTTP: URL path, headers, cookies
Can route byConnection/api/* → API servers, /images/* → static servers
SpeedFaster, less CPUSlower, but smarter
ExtrasNoneTLS termination, compression, auth, rewriting, A/B routing
ExamplesAWS NLB, HAProxy (TCP mode)AWS ALB, Nginx, HAProxy (HTTP mode), Envoy

Algorithms: how the LB picks a server

static
Round robin

1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3… Simple and fair when servers and requests are alike.

static
Weighted round robin

A server twice as big gets twice the turns. Good for mixed hardware.

dynamic
Least connections

Send to whoever is busiest the least. Best when requests take very different times.

dynamic
Least response time

Pick the server answering fastest right now.

hash
IP hash / consistent hash

hash(clientIP) % N: the same user always lands on the same server. Useful for caches and sticky behaviour.

random
Random / power of two choices

Pick two servers at random, use the less loaded one. Surprisingly close to optimal.

LiveLoad balancer simulator

Requests have random durations. Try "Least connections" with a burst and watch how it avoids the busy server. Kill server 3 and see the health check route around it.

Real config: Nginx as a load balancer

Sticky sessions, and who balances the balancer?

Sticky sessions pin a user to one server (via a cookie). It's a quick fix for stateful apps but it breaks even spreading, and the user loses their session when that server dies. Prefer stateless servers (Chapter 2).

A single load balancer is itself a single point of failure. Production setups run two in an active–passive pair sharing a floating virtual IP (keepalived/VRRP), or use a managed LB (AWS ALB) that is already redundant across zones. Across regions, DNS / global server load balancing sends users to the nearest healthy region.

Common trap

Health checks that only check "is the process alive" (/ping returns 200) miss servers that are alive but broken, e.g. lost their DB connection. A good /health checks critical dependencies, but keep it cheap, or the health checks themselves become load.

Lock it in

Bablu at the gate: Spread, Skip the sick, Single front door.

L4 = fast, sees only addresses. L7 = smart, sees URLs and headers. Least-connections when requests vary in length, round robin when they don't, hashing when the same user must land on the same server.

Interview questions

How does a load balancer know a server is down?

Active health checks: it calls /health every few seconds and removes the server after N failures, then re-adds it after M successes. Passive checks: it watches real traffic and marks a server bad after repeated errors or timeouts. Most setups use both.

Where would you put load balancers in a three-tier system?

Between users and web servers, between web/API servers and internal services, and sometimes in front of database read replicas. Each tier then scales independently.

Why is hash(key) % N a problem when N changes?

Changing N (adding or removing a server) remaps almost every key, so caches miss and sessions move all at once. Consistent hashing (Chapter 7) fixes this by remapping only about 1/N of the keys.

Next: Caching and CDNs →
04HLD · Building blocks

Caching and CDNs

A cache keeps a copy of frequently used data somewhere faster and closer, so you don't redo slow work for every request.

At Ramu's chai stall

Brewing each cup from scratch takes 4 minutes. But 80% of customers order the same plain masala chai. So every morning Ramu brews a big batch and keeps it hot in flasks on the counter. A masala chai order is now served in 10 seconds. Rare orders (green tea with honey) are still made fresh.

The flasks are a cache. Finding chai in the flask is a cache hit; having to brew is a cache miss. Throwing out tea older than 2 hours is a TTL (time to live). When the flask shelf is full and he removes the flavour nobody ordered recently, that's LRU eviction.

Where caches live

Caching strategies: who updates the cache, and when

StrategyHow it worksGoodBad
Cache-asideApp reads cache; on miss reads DB and fills cacheSimple; cache failure isn't fatal; only hot data cachedFirst request is slow; data can be stale until TTL
Read-throughCache itself loads from DB on missApp code is simplerNeeds a cache library/provider that supports it
Write-throughEvery write goes to cache and DB togetherCache always freshSlower writes; caches data nobody reads
Write-behind (write-back)Write to cache now, flush to DB later in batchesVery fast writesData loss if cache dies before flushing
Write-aroundWrite only to DB; cache fills on next readAvoids filling cache with write-once dataRecent writes miss the cache

Spring shortcut: the same thing with annotations is @Cacheable("menu") on getMenu and @CacheEvict("menu") on updateMenu, with Redis configured as the cache manager.

Eviction: what to throw out when the cache is full

LRU: Least Recently Used

Remove what hasn't been touched for the longest time. The default choice.

LFU: Least Frequently Used

Remove what's used least often. Good when popularity is stable.

FIFO

Remove the oldest inserted item, regardless of use. Simple, rarely best.

TTL

Every entry expires after a fixed time. Controls staleness rather than space.

LiveLRU cache with capacity 4
Most recent → least recent

LRU is also a classic LLD coding question. The trick: a HashMap for O(1) lookup plus a doubly linked list for O(1) "move to front" and "remove last".

The four classic cache disasters

Stampede (thundering herd)

A hot key expires; 5,000 requests miss at once and all hit the DB.

  • Fix: lock so one request rebuilds, others wait
  • Refresh before expiry; add random jitter to TTLs
Penetration

Requests for keys that don't exist (e.g. id=-1) always miss and always hit the DB.

  • Fix: cache the "not found" result briefly
  • Bloom filter in front (Chapter 15)
Avalanche

Many keys expire at the same moment, or the cache cluster restarts; the DB is flooded.

  • Fix: randomise TTLs
  • Replicated cache cluster, warm-up on start
Hot key

One celebrity key gets millions of reads and overloads a single cache node.

  • Fix: local in-process cache layer
  • Replicate the key as key#1…key#N

CDN: a cache spread across the planet

A Content Delivery Network is a set of servers ("edge locations") in hundreds of cities that keep copies of your static files. A user in Chennai downloads your logo from a Chennai edge server instead of your origin in Mumbai or Virginia.

Pull CDN

Edge fetches from your origin on the first request, then caches it. Easy; first user per region pays the miss. Most common (CloudFront, Cloudflare).

Push CDN

You upload content to the CDN in advance. More control, good for big files that rarely change (videos, game patches).

Bust stale files with versioned file names (app.3f9a2c.js) instead of waiting for TTLs or purging.

Common trap

"Just add a cache" without asking how stale is acceptable? A menu can be 10 minutes old. A bank balance or seat availability usually can't. Caching is a deliberate trade of freshness for speed; say the trade-off out loud.

Lock it in

Flasks on the counter: hit fast, miss once, throw out the stale.

Default answer: cache-aside + TTL + delete-on-write, Redis as the store, LRU eviction. Name the risks: stampede, penetration, avalanche, hot keys. "There are only two hard things in computer science: cache invalidation and naming things."

Interview questions

On a write, why delete the cache key instead of updating it?

Two concurrent writers can update the DB in one order and the cache in the opposite order, leaving the cache permanently wrong. Deleting is idempotent and order-safe: the next read reloads the true value from the DB. (A small race still exists with a concurrent reader; delayed double-delete or short TTLs cover it.)

What should and shouldn't be cached?

Cache data that is read far more than written, expensive to compute, and tolerant of slight staleness: product pages, profiles, feeds, configuration, session data. Be careful with data needing strict correctness (balances, inventory at checkout) or that is unique per request with no reuse.

Redis vs Memcached?

Both are in-memory key-value stores. Redis has rich data types (lists, sets, sorted sets, hashes, streams), persistence, replication, pub/sub and Lua scripts; it's the usual default. Memcached is simpler, multi-threaded and purely a cache of strings, good for very simple high-throughput caching.

Next: Databases: SQL, NoSQL, ACID, indexes →
05HLD · Data

Databases: SQL, NoSQL, ACID and indexes

The database is the source of truth. Choosing the right kind, and using transactions and indexes well, decides whether your data is correct and fast.

At Ramu's chai stall

Ramu keeps a big ledger: customers on one page, orders on another, stock on a third, all with neat columns and cross-references ("Order 512 → Customer 88"). That's a relational (SQL) database.

His nephew runs the Instagram page and just throws each customer's whole story into one folder: name, photos, favourite drinks, comments, all together, every folder shaped a little differently. That's a document (NoSQL) database. Both work. They suit different jobs.

SQL vs NoSQL

SQL (relational)NoSQL (non-relational)
Shape of dataTables with fixed columns; rows linked by foreign keysDocuments, key-value pairs, wide columns or graphs; flexible schema
Query powerRich: JOINs, aggregations, ad-hoc SQLUsually by key or a few fields; JOINs limited or absent
GuaranteesACID transactionsOften BASE (eventual consistency); many now offer ACID per document or more
ScalingScales up easily; scaling out (sharding) is manual workBuilt to scale out across many nodes
ExamplesMySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL ServerMongoDB, Cassandra, DynamoDB, Redis, Neo4j
Pick whenRelationships matter, correctness matters (payments, orders, inventory)Huge scale, flexible/changing shape, simple access patterns (logs, feeds, sessions, IoT)

The four families of NoSQL

key → value
Key-value

A giant hash map. Fastest possible lookups by key.

  • Redis, DynamoDB, Riak
  • Sessions, caches, carts
JSON docs
Document

Self-contained JSON-like documents; query on fields inside.

  • MongoDB, Couchbase, Firestore
  • Catalogues, profiles, CMS
row key → many columns
Wide-column

Rows with huge numbers of columns, partitioned across nodes; very fast writes.

  • Cassandra, HBase, Bigtable
  • Messages, time series, activity logs
nodes + edges
Graph

Relationships are first-class; walking connections is cheap.

  • Neo4j, Amazon Neptune
  • Social graphs, recommendations, fraud rings

Specialists you'll also name in designs: search engines (Elasticsearch, inverted index for full-text search), time-series DBs (InfluxDB, Prometheus), and object stores (S3, for files and blobs).

ACID: the promise of a transaction

A transaction is a group of operations that must succeed or fail together. Example: Priya pays ₹15 by wallet. Two things must happen: her wallet goes down by 15, Ramu's goes up by 15.

A
Atomicity: all or nothing

If the server crashes after debiting Priya but before crediting Ramu, the debit is rolled back. Money never vanishes.

C
Consistency: rules always hold

Constraints (balance ≥ 0, foreign keys, unique email) are true before and after every transaction.

I
Isolation: no peeking at half-done work

Two payments running at once behave as if they ran one after another.

D
Durability: committed means saved

Once the DB says "committed", a power cut won't lose it (write-ahead log on disk).

BASE is the looser NoSQL promise: Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually consistent. Replicas may disagree for a moment but converge.

Isolation levels and the anomalies they prevent

LevelDirty readNon-repeatable readPhantom readNote
Read uncommittedpossiblepossiblepossibleAlmost never used
Read committedpreventedpossiblepossiblePostgreSQL, Oracle default
Repeatable readpreventedpreventedpossible*MySQL InnoDB default (*gap locks block most phantoms)
SerializablepreventedpreventedpreventedSafest, slowest

Dirty read: you see another transaction's uncommitted change. Non-repeatable read: you read the same row twice and get different values. Phantom: you run the same query twice and new rows appear.

Optimistic vs pessimistic locking

Optimistic: "conflicts are rare"

No lock. Read a version number; on update, WHERE version = ?. If someone else changed it, fail and retry. Great for low contention (profile edits).

Pessimistic: "conflicts are likely"

Lock the row while working: SELECT … FOR UPDATE. Others wait. Good for hot rows (last seat on a flight, flash-sale stock).

Indexes: the back-of-the-book index

Finding "Priya" in a 10-million-row table without an index means reading every row (a full table scan). An index is a sorted structure, usually a B+ tree, that points straight to the right rows, the way a book's index points to page numbers.

Common trap

Indexes are not free. Every INSERT/UPDATE must update every index too, and indexes use disk and memory. Index the columns you filter, join and sort on; don't index everything. Low-cardinality columns (gender, boolean flags) alone are usually poor indexes.

Normalise or denormalise?

Normalised

Each fact stored once (customer name lives only in customers). No update anomalies; needs JOINs to read. Default for OLTP systems.

Denormalised

Copy data where it's read (store customer_name inside each order). Fast reads, no JOINs; must keep copies in sync. Common at scale and in NoSQL.

Lock it in

ACID = "All Conditions Isolated, Durable."

SQL when relationships and correctness rule; NoSQL when scale and flexible shape rule. Indexes turn scans into lookups at the cost of slower writes. Use optimistic locking for rare conflicts, pessimistic for hot rows.

Interview questions

How do you choose between SQL and NoSQL for a new feature?

Start from access patterns and guarantees. Need multi-row transactions, joins, ad-hoc reporting, strict integrity? SQL. Need massive write throughput, horizontal scale, a schema that changes often, and access mostly by key? NoSQL. Many systems use both: MySQL for orders and payments, Cassandra for activity logs, Redis for sessions, Elasticsearch for search ("polyglot persistence").

Why can adding an index make a system slower?

Writes must maintain every index, so write-heavy tables slow down; indexes consume buffer-pool memory, pushing hot data out; and the optimiser might pick a poor index. Measure with EXPLAIN and real workloads.

What does @Transactional not protect you from?

Self-invocation (calling a @Transactional method from the same class bypasses the Spring proxy), checked exceptions (no rollback by default), calls to other services or message brokers (those aren't in the DB transaction), and lost updates under the default isolation level unless you add locking.

Next: Replication →
06HLD · Data

Replication: copies of the same data

Replication keeps the same data on several machines so that reads scale, and a dead machine doesn't lose data or stop the service.

At Ramu's chai stall

Ramu now has branches in Kharagpur and Kolkata. Only the head office ledger can be written to (new orders, price changes). Every evening a clerk photocopies the changes and sends them to each branch, so branches can look up prices and loyalty points locally without calling head office.

One day a customer pays at head office and immediately walks into the Kolkata branch asking for his points. The photocopy hasn't arrived yet, so the branch shows his old balance. That's replication lag.

Synchronous vs asynchronous

Synchronous

The leader waits until a follower confirms before saying "committed". No data loss on failover, but every write is as slow as the slowest replica, and a dead replica blocks writes.

Asynchronous

The leader commits immediately and ships changes later. Fast writes, but followers lag, and if the leader dies, the last few writes may be lost.

Semi-synchronous

Wait for at least one follower, the rest async. The common middle ground (MySQL semi-sync, Postgres synchronous_standby_names).

Problems caused by lag, and their fixes

ProblemWhat the user seesFix
Read-your-own-writes"I updated my profile but it still shows the old one"Read your own data from the leader for a short window after writing, or track the write's position and read from a replica that has caught up
Monotonic readsRefresh shows a comment, refresh again and it disappears (hit a more-lagged replica)Pin each user to one replica (hash of user ID)
Consistent prefixSee an answer before the question it replies toWrite causally related data to the same partition

Three replication topologies

Quorum formula

With N replicas, a write waits for W acks and a read asks R replicas. If R + W > N, at least one replica in every read has the latest write. Typical: N=3, W=2, R=2. Tune for speed: W=1 (fast writes, risky) or R=1 (fast reads).

Failover: when the leader dies

  1. DetectFollowers or a monitor (Orchestrator, Patroni, cloud RDS) notice missed heartbeats, typically after 10–30 seconds.
  2. ElectPick the most up-to-date follower as the new leader (consensus such as Raft, or a coordinator like ZooKeeper/etcd).
  3. ReconfigurePoint writes at the new leader (DNS/virtual IP/proxy update); other followers now follow it.
  4. Fence the old leaderIf the old leader comes back thinking it's still in charge, you get split brain: two leaders accepting writes. Fencing tokens or STONITH ("shoot the other node in the head") prevent it.
Lock it in

One pen, many photocopies.

Replication = same data, many machines (for availability and read scale). Sharding = different data, many machines (for write and storage scale). Async replication is fast but laggy; quorum rule R + W > N; beware split brain on failover.

Interview questions

Replication vs backup: why do you need both?

Replication copies every change immediately, including mistakes: a DELETE without a WHERE is replicated to every follower in milliseconds. Backups (and point-in-time recovery from logs) let you go back in time. Replication protects against machine failure; backups protect against human and software error.

A user updates their name and immediately sees the old one. Why, and how do you fix it?

The write went to the leader but the read was served by a lagging replica. Fixes: read the user's own profile from the leader for a few seconds after an edit; or record the leader's log position after the write and only read from replicas that have reached it; or update the UI optimistically on the client.

Next: Sharding and consistent hashing →
07HLD · Data

Sharding and consistent hashing

Sharding splits one big dataset into smaller pieces stored on different machines, so writes and storage can grow beyond what one database can hold.

At Ramu's chai stall

The head-office ledger is now 4,000 pages, and only one clerk can write in it at a time. The queue of clerks waiting to write is longer than the queue of customers. Ramu splits it into three ledgers: surnames A–H, I–P and Q–Z, each with its own clerk. Three clerks now write in parallel.

But then a hundred customers named "Sharma" and "Singh" show up, and the Q–Z clerk is drowning while A–H sits idle. That's a hot shard, and it's why choosing the split (the shard key) is the most important sharding decision.

Ways to choose the shard

StrategyHowStrengthWeakness
Range-basedIDs 1–1M → shard 1, 1M–2M → shard 2; or by dateRange queries are easy; simpleHot spots: all new users/today's data land on the newest shard
Hash-basedshard = hash(user_id) % NEven spread of data and loadRange queries hit every shard; changing N moves most data
Consistent hashingHash keys and servers onto a ringAdding a server moves only ~1/N of keysMore complex; needs virtual nodes for balance
Directory / lookupA lookup table maps key → shardFully flexible; move tenants individuallyThe directory is extra latency and a single point of failure
Geo-basedIndia users → Mumbai shard, EU → FrankfurtLow latency, data residency lawsUneven region sizes

What sharding costs you

Cross-shard queries

"Top 10 customers overall" must ask every shard and merge (scatter–gather).

Cross-shard transactions

No simple ACID across shards. You need sagas or 2PC (Chapter 14).

No cross-shard JOINs

Denormalise, or join in application code.

Resharding

Growing from 4 to 8 shards means moving data live without downtime.

Interview tip

Pick the shard key from the main access pattern. For a chat app: conversation_id, so one conversation's messages live together. For an e-commerce order system: customer_id, so "my orders" hits one shard. Say why, and name the hot-key risk (a celebrity, a giant tenant).

Consistent hashing, drawn

With plain hash(key) % N, going from 4 servers to 5 changes the answer for roughly 80% of keys. Every cache misses at once. Consistent hashing fixes this:

  1. Make a ringImagine hash values 0 … 2³²−1 bent into a circle.
  2. Place serversHash each server's name to a point on the ring.
  3. Place keysHash each key to a point, then walk clockwise to the first server. That server owns the key.
  4. Add a serverIt takes over only the keys between itself and its counter-clockwise neighbour. Everyone else stays put.
  5. Use virtual nodesPlace each physical server at 100–200 points on the ring so the slices are even and a removed server's load spreads over many servers, not one.
LiveConsistent hashing ring vs modulo hashing

60 keys are placed on the ring. Each key takes the colour of the server that owns it. When you add or remove a server, compare how many keys moved on the ring with how many would have moved using hash % N.

Used by: Cassandra and DynamoDB (partitioning), Memcached clients, Discord, Akamai, load balancers doing cache-friendly routing.

Lock it in

Split the ledger, walk clockwise.

Shard when one machine can't hold the writes or the data. Choose the shard key from the main query. Hash for even spread, range for range queries, consistent hashing so adding a node moves only ~1/N keys, virtual nodes for balance.

Interview questions

Partitioning vs sharding vs replication?

Partitioning is splitting data into pieces; when the pieces live on different machines it's usually called sharding (horizontal partitioning). Vertical partitioning splits by columns or by feature (user profile table vs user activity table). Replication copies the same piece to multiple machines. Real systems do both: each shard has its own replicas.

How would you reshard a live MySQL database from 4 to 8 shards?

Use logical shards: hash keys into, say, 1,024 virtual buckets mapped to 4 physical servers. To grow, move whole buckets: copy a bucket's data to the new server, stream ongoing changes (binlog/CDC) until caught up, briefly block writes for that bucket, flip the mapping, then delete the old copy. Tools like Vitess automate this.

Next: CAP, PACELC and consistency →
08HLD · Data

CAP, PACELC and consistency models

When the network between your servers breaks, you must choose: refuse some requests to stay correct, or answer everything and risk being out of date.

At Ramu's chai stall

A storm cuts the phone line between the Kharagpur and Kolkata branches. A customer in Kolkata asks, "How many loyalty points do I have? I want to redeem 100." The Kolkata branch can't check with Kharagpur, where he might have spent points this morning.

Choice 1: "Sorry, our system is down, come back later." Correct but unhelpful. That's choosing Consistency. Choice 2: "Your balance as of last night is 250, enjoy!" Helpful but maybe wrong. That's choosing Availability. He can't have both while the line is cut, and the line cut is the Partition.

C
Consistency

Every read sees the most recent write (or gets an error). All nodes show the same data at the same time.

A
Availability

Every request to a working node gets a non-error response, even if it's not the latest data.

P
Partition tolerance

The system keeps running even when messages between nodes are lost or delayed.

Which to choose?

SystemChoiceWhy
Bank transfer, stock trading, seat bookingCPShowing a wrong balance or selling one seat twice is worse than a short error
Social feed, likes count, product reviewsAPA like count that's 2 seconds old harms nobody; downtime loses users
Shopping cart (Amazon's Dynamo paper)APAlways let people add to cart; merge conflicting carts later
Configuration / leader election (etcd, ZooKeeper)CPTwo nodes both believing they're leader is catastrophic

PACELC: the part CAP forgets

Definition

If Partition: choose A or C. Else (normal operation): choose Latency or Consistency. Even with a healthy network, waiting for replicas to agree makes every request slower.

DynamoDB and Cassandra are PA/EL (available in partitions, fast normally). Traditional SQL with synchronous replicas and Google Spanner are PC/EC (consistent always, paying latency). MongoDB is configurable.

The consistency ladder

Common trap

"We'll pick CA." In a system spread over more than one machine, partitions will happen, so CA isn't a real option. Also, the C in CAP (linearizability) is not the C in ACID (integrity rules). Same letter, different meaning.

Lock it in

Phone line cut? Be Correct or be Kind.

P is forced on you. During a partition choose CP (money, bookings, locks) or AP (feeds, likes, carts). PACELC adds: even without failures, consistency costs latency.

Interview questions

Is Cassandra CP or AP?

By default AP: any replica can accept writes and reads return what that replica has. But it's tunable per query: with QUORUM reads and writes (R + W > N) you get strong consistency for that data, at the cost of availability if too many replicas are unreachable.

For a ticket booking system, which parts are CP and which AP?

Seat reservation and payment are CP: never double-book; it's fine to show "try again". Browsing events, showing approximate seats left, reviews and recommendations are AP: stale by a few seconds is fine, downtime is not. Mixing guarantees per feature is the mature answer.

Next: Message queues and Kafka →
09HLD · Communication

Message queues, pub/sub and Kafka

A message queue lets one part of a system drop off work and move on, while another part picks it up when it's ready. The two never have to wait for each other.

At Ramu's chai stall

At first, the cashier took an order, then stood waiting at the stove until the tea was ready, then served it. During rush hour the line didn't move. So Ramu put up a metal spike: the cashier writes an order slip, sticks it on the spike and immediately serves the next customer. Two cooks pull slips off the spike at their own pace.

At 8 a.m. the spike holds 40 slips. Nobody is turned away; the cooks just catch up by 8:20. The spike is a message queue. The cashier is the producer, the cooks are consumers, and the spike absorbing the rush is called load levelling.

Why queues are everywhere

Decoupling

The producer doesn't know or care who consumes. Add a new "SMS worker" without touching the order service.

Load levelling

Spikes queue up instead of crashing consumers. Consumers work at a steady, safe rate.

Reliability

If a consumer crashes, the message stays in the queue and is retried.

Scaling consumers

Queue growing? Add more workers. They share the messages.

Two shapes: queue and pub/sub

Point-to-point queue

Each message is handled by exactly one consumer, then deleted. Work distribution: "resize this image", "send this email". RabbitMQ queues, AWS SQS.

Publish / subscribe

Each message goes to every subscriber. Event broadcasting: "OrderPlaced" is heard by email, inventory and analytics. Kafka topics, SNS, Redis pub/sub.

Kafka in one picture

Delivery guarantees

GuaranteeMeaningHow it happensRisk
At-most-onceDelivered 0 or 1 timesCommit offset before processingLost messages
At-least-onceDelivered 1 or more timesCommit offset after processing; retry on failureDuplicates; the common default
Exactly-onceEffect happens onceIdempotent consumer, or Kafka transactions within KafkaCostly; true end-to-end needs idempotency anyway

Because at-least-once means duplicates will arrive, consumers must be idempotent: processing the same message twice must have the same effect as once.

Things that go wrong, and the standard fixes

Poison message

A message that always fails blocks or loops forever. After N retries, move it to a dead-letter queue (DLQ) for humans to inspect.

Ordering

Only guaranteed per partition/queue. Use the entity ID (orderId) as the key so its events stay in order.

Backpressure

Consumers falling behind forever? Monitor consumer lag; scale consumers (up to the partition count) or slow producers.

Dual write

Saving to the DB and publishing to Kafka are two systems; one can fail. Use the transactional outbox (Chapter 14).

RabbitMQApache KafkaAWS SQS
ModelSmart broker, queues and exchangesDistributed append-only logManaged simple queue
After readingMessage removed when ackedMessage kept (retention); can replayRemoved when deleted
ThroughputTens of thousands/sMillions/sVery high, managed
Best forTask queues, complex routing, RPCEvent streaming, logs, analytics, event sourcingSimple decoupling on AWS with zero ops
Lock it in

Slip on the spike: Drop it, Decouple, Drain later.

Queue = one consumer per message. Pub/sub = every subscriber gets it. Kafka = partitioned log, ordered per partition, replayable. Assume at-least-once, so make consumers idempotent, and send poison messages to a DLQ.

Interview questions

How many consumers can usefully read a Kafka topic with 6 partitions in one group?

At most 6. Each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer in a group; a 7th consumer sits idle. To scale beyond that, increase partitions (plan this upfront, since changing partition count reshuffles key-to-partition mapping).

When would you not use a queue?

When the user needs the result right now (checking a password, reading a balance), when strict request–response semantics are needed, or when the added infrastructure and eventual consistency aren't worth it for a small system.

Next: APIs: REST, GraphQL, gRPC, WebSockets →
10HLD · Communication

APIs: REST, GraphQL, gRPC and real-time

An API is the contract between two pieces of software: what you can ask for, how to ask, and what you'll get back.

At Ramu's chai stall

Ramu paints a menu board: "Masala chai ₹15. Elaichi chai ₹20. Add ginger +₹5." Customers don't need to know how the stove works; they just order from the board. When Ramu changes his recipe, the board stays the same, so nobody is confused. That board is an API: a stable contract that hides the kitchen.

REST: resources and verbs

REST treats everything as a resource (a noun with a URL) and uses HTTP methods as the verbs.

Avoid (verbs in URLs)Prefer (RESTful)Returns
POST /createOrderPOST /orders201 Created + Location header
GET /getOrder?id=42GET /orders/42200 or 404
POST /updateSugarPATCH /orders/42200
GET /getOrdersOfUser?u=7GET /users/7/orders?status=PAID&limit=20200 + page
POST /deleteOrderDELETE /orders/42204 No Content

Production API habits

Versioning

/v1/orders or a header. Never break existing clients; add fields, don't rename them.

Pagination

Offset (?page=5) is simple but slow and shifts when rows are added. Cursor (?after=ord_981) is stable and fast for feeds.

Idempotency keys

Client sends Idempotency-Key: uuid with a POST; the server stores the result and returns it again on retry. Stripe-style safe payments.

Consistent errors

Correct status codes and a body like {"code":"OUT_OF_STOCK","message":"…"}.

REST vs GraphQL vs gRPC

RESTGraphQLgRPC
ShapeMany URLs, fixed responsesOne endpoint; client writes a query for exactly the fields it wantsRemote function calls defined in .proto files
FormatJSON over HTTP/1.1 or 2JSON over HTTPBinary Protobuf over HTTP/2
StrengthSimple, cacheable, universalNo over-fetching/under-fetching; great for varied UIsVery fast, strongly typed, streaming both ways
WeaknessOver-fetching; many round trips for nested dataHard to cache; complex queries can be expensive (N+1)Not browser-friendly; binary is hard to debug
Use forPublic APIs, CRUDMobile/web front ends aggregating many sourcesInternal service-to-service calls

Real-time: how the server talks first

Lock it in

Nouns in the URL, verbs in the method.

REST for public and CRUD, GraphQL for flexible front ends, gRPC for fast internal calls. Real-time ladder: poll → long-poll → SSE → WebSocket. Always: version, paginate (cursor for feeds), and use idempotency keys on POSTs that move money.

Interview questions

How would you design pagination for an infinite-scroll feed?

Cursor-based: return items plus an opaque next_cursor (e.g. encoded last created_at + id). The next query is WHERE (created_at, id) < (cursor) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20, which uses an index and doesn't skip or repeat items when new posts arrive. Offset pagination gets slower with depth and shifts under inserts.

WebSocket at scale: what's hard?

Connections are long-lived and stateful, so each server holds many open sockets (memory, file descriptors); load balancers must support upgrades and long timeouts; to message a user you must know which server holds their socket (a connection registry in Redis, or pub/sub between servers); and reconnect storms after a deploy need jittered backoff.

Next: Monolith vs microservices →
11HLD · Architecture

Monolith vs microservices

A monolith is one deployable app that does everything; microservices split it into small services, each owning one business capability and its own data.

At Ramu's chai stall

In the original stall, Ramu did everything at one counter: tea, samosas, billing, deliveries. Easy to manage, one place to look. But when the samosa fryer catches fire, the whole stall shuts. And hiring a samosa specialist means retraining him on tea and billing too.

The flagship store now has separate counters: a tea counter, a snacks counter, a billing counter and a delivery desk. Each has its own staff, its own stock and its own hours. If snacks close, tea keeps selling. A front desk greets everyone and sends them to the right counter. That front desk is the API gateway.

MonolithMicroservices
DeployEverything togetherEach service independently, many times a day
ScalingScale the whole appScale only the hot service (e.g. search)
FailureA memory leak in one module can take down allFailures can be contained (with timeouts and circuit breakers)
DataOne DB, easy JOINs and ACIDDB per service; cross-service consistency via sagas/events
ComplexityLow ops; can become a "big ball of mud"Network calls, distributed tracing, versioning, DevOps maturity needed
TeamsFine for small teamsFits many teams owning separate domains (Conway's Law)

The supporting cast of a microservice system

API Gateway

Single entry: routing, auth, rate limiting, TLS, request aggregation. Spring Cloud Gateway, Kong, AWS API Gateway.

Service discovery

Services register where they run; others look them up by name, not IP. Eureka, Consul, Kubernetes DNS.

Config server

Central, versioned configuration and secrets. Spring Cloud Config, Vault.

Service mesh

A sidecar proxy next to each service handles retries, mTLS and metrics without code changes. Istio, Linkerd.

Backend for Frontend

A thin API per client type (mobile BFF, web BFF) shaping data for that UI.

Observability

Centralised logs, metrics and distributed traces with a correlation ID across services (Chapter 17).

Common trap

The distributed monolith: services that share one database or must all deploy together. You get all the pain of microservices and none of the benefits. Also, splitting too early: start with a well-structured modular monolith and extract services along clear domain boundaries (DDD bounded contexts) when a team or scaling need justifies it.

Lock it in

Separate counters, separate stock, one front desk.

Microservice = one business capability, own data, independent deploy. Pay for it with network calls, eventual consistency and ops tooling. Monolith first is not a failure; it's usually the right start.

Interview questions

How do you decide service boundaries?

Follow business domains (Domain-Driven Design bounded contexts): Orders, Payments, Catalogue, Shipping. A good service has high cohesion inside, few calls outside, owns its data, and can be owned by one team. If two services always change together or need constant synchronous chatter, they probably belong together.

Sync (REST/gRPC) or async (events) between services?

Use sync when the caller needs an answer to continue (check stock before showing checkout). Use async events for side effects and for spreading information (OrderPlaced → email, analytics, loyalty). Async reduces coupling and cascading failures; sync is simpler to reason about. Most systems mix both.

Next: Rate limiting →
12HLD · Protection

Rate limiting

A rate limiter caps how many requests a client may make in a period of time, protecting the system from abuse, accidents and overload.

At Ramu's chai stall

A reseller starts buying 200 cups at a time and selling them outside the station at double the price. Regular customers find the flasks empty. Ramu puts up a sign: "Maximum 5 cups per person per 10 minutes." Bablu at the gate gives each person 5 tokens; every cup costs a token; tokens come back slowly over time. When you're out of tokens, you wait.

That's the token bucket algorithm, the most widely used rate limiter.

Why rate limit?

Stop abuse

Brute-force logins, scraping, DDoS.

Fairness

One noisy tenant can't starve everyone else.

Protect downstream

Your DB or a paid third-party API can only take so much.

Cost control

Free tier = 100 calls/day; paid tier = more.

Five algorithms

AlgorithmHowProsCons
Token bucketTokens refill at rate r up to capacity b; each request takes oneAllows bursts; memory-light; used by AWS, StripeTwo parameters to tune
Leaky bucketQueue drains at constant rateSmooth, steady outputBursts wait or drop; old requests can block new
Fixed window counterCount per calendar minute; reset at :00Simplest (Redis INCR)Edge burst: 100 at 0:59 + 100 at 1:00 = 200 in 2 s
Sliding window logStore each request's timestamp; count those in the last 60 sExactMemory per request
Sliding window counterCurrent window + weighted previous windowClose to exact, cheapApproximation
LiveToken bucket: capacity 5, refill 1 token every 1.5 s

5 / 5 tokens

Distributed rate limiting

With 20 API servers, each keeping its own bucket, a user could get 20× the limit. Keep counters in Redis, shared by all servers, and make the check-and-increment atomic with a Lua script (or INCR + EXPIRE for a fixed window).

Interview tip

Say where the limiter lives (API gateway is typical), what key it limits by (user ID, API key, IP for anonymous traffic), what happens on reject (429 + Retry-After), and what happens if Redis is down (usually fail open: allow traffic rather than block every user).

Lock it in

Tokens drip in, requests spend them.

Token bucket = bursts OK, average capped. Leaky bucket = smooth output. Fixed window = simple but edge bursts. Sliding window = accurate. Share counters in Redis with atomic ops across servers.

Interview questions

Design a rate limiter for an API used by 10 million users.

Put it in the API gateway as middleware. Rules (per user/API key/endpoint) come from a config store and are cached locally. Counters live in a Redis cluster sharded by key; use a token bucket or sliding window counter via an atomic Lua script. Return 429 with Retry-After and rate-limit headers. For latency, consider a small local pre-check and async syncing for non-critical limits. Monitor rejected counts; fail open if Redis is unreachable.

What's the fixed-window edge problem?

A limit of 100/minute resets at each minute boundary, so a client can send 100 requests at 12:00:59 and another 100 at 12:01:00, i.e. 200 within two seconds. Sliding windows fix this.

Next: Reliability and fault tolerance →
13HLD · Protection

Reliability and fault tolerance

Everything fails eventually. Reliable systems expect failure and are designed so one broken part doesn't take down the rest.

At Ramu's chai stall

Ramu keeps a spare gas cylinder (redundancy). When the milk supplier is late, he doesn't make customers wait forever; after 5 minutes he serves black tea instead (timeout and fallback). When the supplier has been late three days in a row, Ramu stops calling him altogether for a week and buys from the shop next door, checking back occasionally (circuit breaker). And he keeps the samosa fryer on a separate gas line, so a fryer problem can't cut the gas to the tea stove (bulkhead).

Availability in nines

AvailabilityDowntime per yearPer monthTypical for
99% ("two nines")3.65 days7.3 hoursInternal tools
99.9%8.76 hours43.8 minutesMost SaaS products
99.99%52.6 minutes4.4 minutesPayments, major platforms
99.999%5.3 minutes26 secondsTelecom, core infrastructure

Components in a chain multiply: three services each at 99.9% give 0.999³ ≈ 99.7%. Redundant copies in parallel add up: two independent 99% servers give 1 − 0.01² = 99.99%.

The resilience toolkit

Redundancy

No single point of failure: at least two of everything, across availability zones. Active–active (both serve) or active–passive (standby takes over).

Timeouts

Never wait forever. Every network call gets a timeout shorter than the caller's own deadline.

Retries with backoff + jitter

Retry transient errors, waiting 100 ms, 200 ms, 400 ms… plus randomness, so clients don't retry in sync.

Circuit breaker

After repeated failures, stop calling a sick service for a while and fail fast.

Bulkhead

Separate thread pools/connection pools per dependency so one slow dependency can't exhaust everything.

Fallback & graceful degradation

Show cached recommendations, hide the reviews widget, but keep checkout working.

Load shedding

When overloaded, reject low-priority work early (503) to keep high-priority work alive.

Idempotency

Makes retries safe. Without it, retries cause duplicates.

Circuit breaker, step by step

LiveCircuit breaker: opens after 3 failures in a row, half-opens after 5 s
Closedcalling the supplier
Openfailing fast, using fallback
Half-opentrying one test call

Disaster recovery: RPO and RTO

RPO
Recovery Point Objective

How much data can you afford to lose? "At most 5 minutes of orders." Drives backup/replication frequency.

RTO
Recovery Time Objective

How long can you be down? "Back within 1 hour." Drives standby strategy: backup-restore → pilot light → warm standby → multi-region active-active.

Lock it in

"Two of everything, Time out, Back off, Break the circuit, Build bulkheads."

Retries without timeouts, backoff + jitter and idempotency make outages worse. The circuit breaker is a fuse: Closed → Open → Half-open. Always have a degraded mode.

Interview questions

What is a cascading failure and how do you prevent it?

One slow service causes its callers' threads to pile up waiting, so they slow down, and their callers too, until everything is down. Prevent with timeouts on every call, circuit breakers, bulkheads (separate pools), load shedding and async communication where possible.

Why add jitter to exponential backoff?

Without jitter, all clients that failed at the same moment retry at the same moments (100 ms, 200 ms, 400 ms…), creating synchronized waves that hit the recovering service. Randomness spreads retries out.

Next: Distributed transactions: 2PC, Saga, Outbox, CQRS →
14HLD · Data across services

Distributed transactions: 2PC, Saga, Outbox, CQRS

When one business action touches several services or databases, you can't use a single ACID transaction. These patterns keep the overall result correct anyway.

At Ramu's chai stall

A wedding party orders: 500 cups of tea from Ramu, sweets from Mishra Sweets, and chairs from the tent house. It must be all or nothing; tea without chairs is useless.

Plan A, the strict planner: calls all three, "Can you reserve for Saturday? Don't confirm yet." When all three say yes, he calls again, "Confirm." If any says no, he tells everyone "Cancel." That's two-phase commit. But if the planner's phone dies between the calls, everyone waits, holding stock, unsure.

Plan B, the practical planner: books tea (done), books sweets (done), tries chairs (fails), then calls Mishra and Ramu to undo their bookings. That's a saga with compensating actions.

Two-phase commit (2PC)

Saga: a chain of local transactions with undo steps

StepServiceActionCompensation (undo)
1OrderCreate order (PENDING)Mark order CANCELLED
2PaymentCharge ₹500Refund ₹500
3InventoryReserve 500 cups of stockRelease stock
4DeliveryAssign a delivery slotFree the slot
5OrderMark order CONFIRMED(final step, nothing to undo)

If step 4 fails, run compensations backwards: release stock (3), refund (2), cancel order (1).

Transactional outbox: never lose an event

Common bug: save the order to MySQL, then publish OrderCreated to Kafka. If the app crashes between the two, the order exists but nobody hears about it. Or Kafka succeeds and the DB commit fails, and everyone hears about an order that doesn't exist.

CQRS and event sourcing

CQRS
Command Query Responsibility Segregation

Use one model for writes (normalised, validated) and a different, denormalised model for reads (e.g. an Elasticsearch index or a pre-joined table), kept in sync by events. Great when reads and writes look very different or scale very differently.

Event sourcing
Store the history, not the state

Like a bank passbook: you store every event (Deposited 500, Withdrew 200) and compute the balance by replaying. Full audit trail and time travel; harder queries and schema evolution. Often paired with CQRS.

Lock it in

2PC asks "ready?" then "go!". Saga does, then undoes.

Microservices default to sagas (eventual consistency + compensations), the outbox to publish events reliably, and idempotent consumers. 2PC only where strong atomicity across a few tightly coupled DBs is essential.

Interview questions

What's the weakness of sagas compared with ACID?

No isolation: other transactions can see intermediate states (order PENDING, payment taken, stock not yet reserved). You handle this with semantic locks (a PENDING status others respect), commutative updates, re-reading values, and designing compensations carefully, since some actions (a sent email) can't be undone, only followed by a correction.

When is CQRS overkill?

For simple CRUD where reads and writes use the same shape and modest scale. CQRS adds eventual consistency between the write and read models, more infrastructure and more code. Use it when read patterns are complex or much heavier than writes.

Next: The toolbox: IDs, Bloom filters, geo, search, storage →
15HLD · Toolbox

The toolbox: IDs, Bloom filters, geo, search and storage

Small, clever building blocks that show up again and again in design interviews. Know what each one is for and its one-line trade-off.

1. Unique IDs at scale: Snowflake

A single MySQL AUTO_INCREMENT breaks with many shards (two shards both produce id 1001). UUIDs are unique but 128 bits, random (bad for B-tree index locality) and not time-sortable. Twitter's Snowflake packs a time-sortable, unique 64-bit ID that any server can generate without coordination:

2. Bloom filter: "definitely not" or "probably yes"

A tiny bit array plus k hash functions that answers "have I seen this before?" using very little memory. False positives are possible; false negatives never happen.

Uses: skip a disk lookup for keys that don't exist (Cassandra, HBase), stop cache penetration, "username taken?" pre-checks, web crawler "already visited this URL?", Medium's "already recommended".

3. Geospatial: "find drivers within 2 km"

Geohash

Encode latitude/longitude into a string like tdr1y; nearby places share a prefix. Query your cell and its 8 neighbours. Redis GEOADD/GEOSEARCH uses this idea.

Quadtree

Recursively split the map into 4 squares until each has at most N points. Dense cities get small cells, empty areas big ones.

Uber H3 / Google S2

Hexagonal or spherical cell systems used in production ride-hailing and maps.

4. Search: the inverted index

5. Keeping a cluster together

Heartbeats

Nodes send "I'm alive" every few seconds; missing several marks a node dead.

Gossip protocol

Each node tells a few random others what it knows; news spreads like rumours to all nodes in O(log N) rounds. Cassandra membership.

Leader election & consensus

Raft/Paxos let nodes agree on one leader and one log order, even if some fail (needs a majority). etcd, ZooKeeper, Kafka KRaft.

Distributed lock

Ensure only one worker runs a job: Redis SET key val NX PX 30000, or ZooKeeper/etcd leases. Use fencing tokens for safety.

6. Kinds of storage

TypeThink of it asExamplesUse for
Block storageA raw hard disk attached to one machineAWS EBS, SANDatabase data files, OS disks
File storageA shared folder with directoriesNFS, AWS EFSShared files between servers, legacy apps
Object storageAn infinite bucket of files, each with a key and metadata, via HTTPAWS S3, GCS, MinIOImages, videos, backups, data lakes; cheap and durable

Pattern you will draw constantly: store the file in object storage, store its URL/key in the database, serve it through a CDN. Upload directly from the client using a pre-signed URL so your servers don't carry the bytes.

7. Batch vs stream processing

Batch

Process a large, bounded dataset on a schedule (nightly reports, ML training). Hadoop MapReduce, Spark.

Stream

Process events continuously as they arrive (fraud detection, live dashboards). Kafka Streams, Flink, Spark Streaming.

Lock it in

Snowflake for IDs, Bloom for "no", Geohash for "near", Inverted index for "find".

Files go to object storage + CDN, with only the URL in the DB. Clusters agree through heartbeats, gossip and consensus (Raft).

Interview questions

Why can't a Bloom filter delete items, and what's the fix?

Clearing a bit might also clear it for other items that hashed to the same bit, causing false negatives. A counting Bloom filter stores small counters instead of bits, so deletes decrement them.

How do you serve "nearby restaurants" quickly?

Index restaurant locations by geohash (or quadtree). For a user, compute their geohash at a precision matching the search radius, fetch candidates in that cell plus its neighbours, then compute exact distances and rank. Restaurant locations rarely change, so the index can be cached heavily.

Next: Security: AuthN, AuthZ, JWT, OAuth →
16HLD · Security

Security: authentication, authorization, JWT and OAuth

Authentication asks "who are you?"; authorization asks "what are you allowed to do?" Every design should say how both happen.

At Ramu's chai stall

The flagship store's kitchen has a back door. Staff show an ID card to the guard to enter (authentication). Inside, a cook can use the stove but not open the cash safe; only the manager can (authorization, by role). Visitors get a wristband stamped with their access and an expiry time, so the guard doesn't phone the office every time; he just checks the stamp is genuine. That wristband is a JWT.

Sessions vs tokens (JWT)

Server session + cookieJWT (JSON Web Token)
What the client holdsA random session IDA signed token containing user ID, roles, expiry
Server work per requestLook up the session in Redis/DBVerify the signature; no lookup
Logout / revokeEasy: delete the sessionHard: valid until expiry (use short expiry + refresh tokens, or a denylist)
ScalingNeeds a shared session storeStateless; any service can verify
Good forClassic web appsAPIs, mobile apps, microservices

OAuth 2.0: "Login with Google", step by step

  1. RedirectYour app sends the user to Google's login page with your client ID and the permissions (scopes) you want.
  2. User consentsThe user logs in at Google (your app never sees the password) and approves.
  3. Authorization codeGoogle redirects back to your app with a short-lived code.
  4. ExchangeYour backend swaps the code (plus its client secret, or PKCE verifier for mobile/SPA) for an access token, and with OpenID Connect an ID token saying who the user is.
  5. UseYour app creates its own session or JWT for the user and may call Google APIs with the access token.

OAuth 2.0 is about authorization (granting access); OpenID Connect adds authentication (identity) on top.

Common attacks and the standard defence

AttackWhat happensDefence
SQL injectionUser input changes your SQL: ' OR '1'='1Parameterised queries / JPA, never string concatenation
XSSAttacker's script runs in other users' browsersEscape output, Content-Security-Policy, HttpOnly cookies
CSRFAnother site makes your logged-in browser send a requestCSRF tokens, SameSite cookies
Credential stuffing / brute forceLeaked passwords tried at scaleRate limiting, MFA, lockouts, bcrypt/argon2 hashing
DDoSFlood of trafficCDN/WAF (Cloudflare, AWS Shield), rate limits, autoscaling
Man-in-the-middleTraffic read or changed in transitHTTPS/TLS everywhere, HSTS, mTLS between services
Lock it in

ID card at the door (AuthN), keys to the rooms (AuthZ), stamped wristband (JWT).

HTTPS everywhere, hash passwords with bcrypt, parameterise SQL, short-lived tokens + refresh tokens, least privilege (RBAC). JWTs are signed, not secret.

Interview questions

How would you handle auth across 20 microservices?

Authenticate once at the edge (API gateway or an auth service via OAuth2/OIDC). Issue short-lived JWTs signed with a private key; services verify with the public key (JWKS) without calling the auth service. Pass the user identity downstream; use mTLS or a service mesh for service-to-service trust; enforce authorization (roles/scopes) in each service for its own resources.

How do you log out a user who has a JWT?

Keep access tokens short (5–15 minutes) and use refresh tokens stored server-side; logout revokes the refresh token. For immediate revocation, keep a small denylist of token IDs (jti) in Redis until they expire, or a per-user "tokens valid after" timestamp.

Next: Observability: logs, metrics, traces, SLOs →
17HLD · Operations

Observability: logs, metrics, traces and SLOs

Observability means you can tell what your system is doing, and why, from the outside, without adding new code every time something breaks.

At Ramu's chai stall

With 40 branches, Ramu can't watch every stove. So he installs a dashboard showing cups sold per minute and average wait time (metrics), keeps a complaints diary at every branch (logs), and gives each big catering order a token number that every counter writes down, so he can see exactly where order #7781 got stuck (tracing). He also promises customers "95% of chai served within 3 minutes" (SLO).

pillar 1
Logs

Timestamped records of events: "payment failed for order 7781: card declined". Structured JSON, centralised (ELK, Loki, CloudWatch). Answer "what exactly happened?"

pillar 2
Metrics

Numbers over time: requests/s, error %, p99 latency, CPU. Cheap to store, great for dashboards and alerts (Prometheus + Grafana). Answer "is something wrong?"

pillar 3
Traces

One request's journey across services, as a tree of timed spans sharing a trace ID (OpenTelemetry, Jaeger, Zipkin). Answer "where is it slow?"

SLI, SLO, SLA and the error budget

SLI · indicator
What you measure

"Percentage of requests faster than 300 ms", "percentage of successful requests".

SLO · objective
Your internal target

"99.9% of requests succeed over 30 days."

SLA · agreement
The contract with customers

"99.5% uptime or you get a 10% refund." Always looser than the SLO.

error budget
Allowed failure

99.9% SLO = 0.1% budget ≈ 43 minutes/month. Budget left? Ship features. Budget spent? Focus on reliability.

The four golden signals (Google SRE): Latency, Traffic, Errors, Saturation. Alert on symptoms users feel (error rate, latency SLO burn), not on every CPU spike.

Lock it in

Metrics say "something's wrong", traces say "where", logs say "why".

Golden signals: Latency, Traffic, Errors, Saturation. SLI is the measurement, SLO the target, SLA the promise with penalties; the gap is your error budget.

Interview questions

What would you put on the dashboard for a new service?

Request rate, error rate (by status code), latency p50/p95/p99 per endpoint, saturation (CPU, memory, thread pool and DB connection pool usage, queue lag), dependency health (calls, errors, latency to DB/cache/other services), and business metrics (orders per minute). Alerts on SLO burn rate rather than raw thresholds.

Next: Back-of-the-envelope estimation →
18HLD · Interview skill

Back-of-the-envelope estimation

Rough maths that tells you whether you need 1 server or 1,000, one database or a sharded cluster, before you draw a single box.

At Ramu's chai stall

Before opening at the new airport, Ramu estimates: 30,000 passengers a day, maybe 1 in 10 buys chai, so 3,000 cups. Most come in the 6–9 a.m. rush, so roughly 1,000 cups an hour at peak, about 17 a minute. One person can serve 4 a minute, so he needs 5 counter staff in the morning. He didn't need exact numbers, just the right order of magnitude.

Numbers to carry in your head

Time
  • 1 day = 86,400 s ≈ 105 s
  • 1 month ≈ 2.5 million s
  • 1 year ≈ 3 × 107 s
Data sizes
  • KB = 103, MB = 106, GB = 109, TB = 1012, PB = 1015 bytes
  • 210 ≈ 1 thousand, 220 ≈ 1 million, 230 ≈ 1 billion
Typical sizes
  • A tweet-like text row: ~300 B – 1 KB
  • Compressed photo: ~200 KB – 2 MB
  • 1 minute of HD video: ~50–100 MB
Rough capacity
  • One app server: ~1,000–5,000 simple req/s
  • One MySQL: a few thousand writes/s, ~10K+ simple reads/s
  • One Redis node: ~100K ops/s

Worked example: "ChaiTalk", a short-post social app

Assumptions (always state them aloud): 50 million daily active users; each posts 2 times and reads 100 posts a day; a post is ~500 bytes; 10% of posts carry a 200 KB photo; read:write ratio is high; peak traffic is about 3× average.

QuantityCalculationResult
Write QPS (avg)50M × 2 = 100M posts/day ÷ 105 s~1,000 /s (peak ~3,000)
Read QPS (avg)50M × 100 = 5B reads/day ÷ 105 s~50,000 /s (peak ~150,000)
Text storage per day100M × 500 B50 GB/day → ~18 TB/year
Photo storage per day10M × 200 KB2 TB/day → ~730 TB/year
App servers at peak150,000 ÷ ~1,500 per server~100 servers
Cache for hot posts20% of a day's posts: 0.2 × 50 GB~10 GB → a small Redis cluster
Photo egress50K reads/s × 20% with photo × 200 KB~2 GB/s → must use a CDN

What the numbers told us: reads dominate 50:1, so design for reads (caching, replicas, precomputed feeds). Text fits a sharded database; photos go to object storage with a CDN. 100 servers means a load balancer and stateless services. That's the whole architecture's skeleton, from five minutes of arithmetic.

Interview tip

Round aggressively (86,400 → 100,000), write the steps on the board, and say what each number implies for the design. Interviewers grade reasoning, not precision. Don't spend more than about 5 minutes here.

Lock it in

A day is 105 seconds. Users × actions ÷ 105 = QPS. Peak ≈ 2–3×.

Then storage = items/day × size × retention, and bandwidth = QPS × size. Every number should end with "…so we need X".

Next: The HLD interview framework →
19HLD · Interview playbook

The HLD interview framework

A system design interview is a guided conversation, not a quiz. A fixed sequence of steps keeps you calm and makes sure you cover what interviewers grade.

At Ramu's chai stall

When a hotel asks Ramu to run its breakfast tea service, he doesn't start buying kettles. He asks: How many guests? What time? Only tea, or coffee too? Any VIP floor? Then he estimates, sketches the setup (one central boiler, three serving points, a runner), and only then worries about details like what happens if the boiler fails. Ask, estimate, sketch, deepen.

  1. Clarify requirementsFunctional: what must users be able to do? Pick 3–4 core features and say what's out of scope. Non-functional: scale (users, data), latency targets, availability, consistency needs, read/write ratio, geography.
  2. EstimateQPS (average and peak), storage over 5 years, bandwidth, cache size (Chapter 18). Conclude: "read-heavy, so…".
  3. Define the API and data model3–5 endpoints with parameters. Main entities, keys and which database type, justified by access patterns.
  4. Draw the high-level designClient → (CDN) → LB → services → cache → DB, plus queues and workers. Walk through one write and one read request end to end.
  5. Deep-diveThe interviewer will steer you, or you pick the hardest parts: the ID scheme, the feed fan-out, sharding key, consistency of payments, hot keys, failure handling.
  6. Wrap upName bottlenecks and single points of failure, how you'd monitor it, and what you'd do at 10× scale.

Non-functional checklist

Scale

DAU, QPS, data volume, growth rate.

Performance

Latency targets (p99), real-time needs.

Availability

How many nines; multi-region?

Consistency

Strong (money) or eventual (likes)?

Durability

Can we ever lose data?

Security & compliance

Auth, PII, data residency.

Phrases that signal seniority

"The trade-off here is…"

Every choice costs something. Name it.

"Given it's read-heavy, I'd…"

Tie decisions back to the requirements and numbers.

"Let's start simple, then scale."

A single-server version first, then evolve it.

"If this component fails…"

Proactively discuss failure modes.

Common trap

Jumping into Kafka, Kubernetes and sharding in minute two, before knowing the scale. Or staying silent while drawing. Or going deep on one component and never finishing the end-to-end picture. Breadth first, then depth.

Lock it in

"Real Engineers Always Draw Diagrams Wisely"

Requirements → Estimation → API & data → Design (high-level) → Deep dives → Wrap-up.

Next: Case study: URL shortener →
20HLD · Case study

Case study: design a URL shortener

Turn a long URL into a short code like chai.ly/aZ3kP9q and redirect anyone who opens it. The most common first HLD question, walked through with the framework.

Step 1 · Requirements

Functional
  • Create a short URL for a long URL
  • Redirect short → long
  • Optional custom alias and expiry
  • Click analytics (counts)
Non-functional
  • Very low redirect latency (< 50 ms)
  • Highly available: broken links are unacceptable
  • Codes not guessable in sequence
  • Read-heavy (~100 reads per write)

Step 2 · Estimation

QuantityWorkingResult
New URLs10M/day ÷ 105~100 writes/s
Redirects100 × writes = 1B/day ÷ 105~10,000 reads/s (peak ~30K)
Storage10M × 500 B × 365 × 5 years~9 TB over 5 years
Code lengthBase62 (a–z, A–Z, 0–9): 627≈ 3.5 trillion codes: 7 chars is plenty
Cache20% of daily hot links: 0.2 × 1B reads hit ~few M URLs × 500 Ba few GB in Redis

Step 3 · API and data model

301 or 302? 301 (permanent) lets browsers cache the redirect, which saves load but hides repeat clicks from analytics. 302 (temporary) sends every click through you, so analytics are accurate. Most shorteners with analytics use 302.

Data model: one main table, accessed purely by key. A key-value / wide-column store (DynamoDB, Cassandra) or sharded MySQL keyed by code both work.

Step 4 · High-level design

Step 5 · Deep dive: generating the short code

ApproachHowProsCons
Hash the URLMD5/SHA-256 of the long URL, take first 7 base62 charsSame URL → same code (dedup)Collisions: must check DB and re-hash; the extra read costs latency
Counter + Base62Unique numeric ID (Snowflake, or a DB/ZooKeeper range allocator) → encode in base62No collisions, ever; short codesSequential codes are guessable (scramble with a bijective shuffle); needs a reliable ID source
Pre-generated keys (KGS)A service pre-creates random unused codes and hands out batchesFast, random, collision-freeExtra service; must not hand the same batch to two servers

A solid answer: range-based counter. Each shorten-service instance asks the KGS for a block of 1,000 IDs (e.g. 5,000,000–5,000,999), uses them from memory, and asks again when it runs out. No coordination per request; a crash just wastes the rest of a block.

Other deep dives worth mentioning

Caching

Links follow a power law: a few go viral. Cache-aside in Redis with LRU; most redirects never touch the DB.

Custom aliases

Insert with a uniqueness check (conditional put / unique key); reject if taken.

Expiry

Check expires_at on read (lazy), plus a background job to delete expired rows. Use DB TTL if supported.

Abuse

Rate-limit creation per user/IP; scan long URLs against malware lists.

Availability

Replicate the DB across zones; the redirect path depends only on cache + DB read replicas.

Analytics

Click events → Kafka → aggregators → a columnar store (ClickHouse). Never on the redirect's critical path.

Lock it in

7 chars of Base62, counter in ranges, cache the hot links, 302 for analytics.

Read-heavy (100:1) → separate read path, aggressive caching. Codes from a collision-free ID source + Base62. Analytics asynchronously through a queue.

Next: Case studies: chat app and news feed →
21HLD · Case study

Case studies: a chat app and a news feed

Two classics that test real-time delivery and fan-out. Same building blocks as before, assembled differently.

A. Design a chat app (WhatsApp-style)

Requirements
  • 1:1 and group chats (up to 256)
  • Delivered and read receipts
  • Messages reach offline users when they return
  • Online/last-seen presence
  • History synced across devices
Key numbers
  • 500M DAU × 40 messages/day = 20B/day
  • ≈ 200K messages/s avg, ~600K peak
  • ~100 bytes each → ~2 TB/day of text
  • Hundreds of millions of open connections
  1. SendAsha's app sends the message (with a client-generated ID for dedup) over her WebSocket to chat server 7.
  2. Persist and ackThe message gets a time-sortable ID and is written to the message store; Asha sees one tick (sent).
  3. LocateThe router looks up Bikram in the session registry: he's on chat server 3.
  4. DeliverServer 3 pushes it down Bikram's socket; his app acks; Asha sees two ticks (delivered). If Bikram is offline, a push notification is sent and the message waits; when he reconnects, his app syncs everything after its last-seen message ID.
  5. Read receiptWhen Bikram opens the chat, a "read" event flows back the same way (blue ticks).

Groups: the router fans a message out to each member's server (small groups) via Kafka. Ordering is per chat, guaranteed by keying Kafka partitions and Cassandra partitions by chat_id. End-to-end encryption means servers store only ciphertext.

B. Design a news feed (Instagram/Twitter-style)

The core question: when Priya opens the app, how do we build her feed of posts from the 300 people she follows, in under 200 ms?

Push (fan-out on write)Pull (fan-out on read)Hybrid (what big apps do)
Write costHigh (one insert per follower)LowPush for normal users
Read costVery low (feed is precomputed)High (merge many timelines)Pull for celebrities, merge at read time
ProblemCelebrity posts, inactive followersSlow feed for users following manyMore complex, but balanced
