Storage pattern: each user's feed is a Redis sorted set of post IDs scored by time (keep the latest ~800). The feed service reads IDs, then hydrates post details from a post cache, and ranks them (recency, affinity, engagement).

Lock it in

Chat: sockets + registry + per-chat order. Feed: push for most, pull for celebrities.

Real-time = WebSockets with a user → server registry. Feeds = hybrid fan-out with precomputed sorted sets in Redis.

Interview questions

How do you guarantee message ordering in a chat?

Order only matters within a conversation. Assign each message a monotonically increasing ID per chat (or a time-sortable Snowflake ID plus a per-chat sequence), route all messages of a chat through the same Kafka partition, and store them in a partition keyed by chat ID sorted by message ID. Clients render by that ID, not by arrival time.

How do you avoid fanning out to inactive users?

Only push into feeds of users active recently (say, the last 30 days). Inactive users get their feed built by pull when they return. This cuts write amplification dramatically.

Next: Part 2 · Real-world architectures →

Part 2 · Chapters 22 to 25

How the giants do it

Netflix, UPI, Stripe and JioHotstar each face a different kind of "huge": huge files, huge transaction counts, huge reliability demands and huge sudden spikes. Every chapter here maps their design back to the building blocks you already know.

How Netflix worksHow UPI works and scalesHow Stripe handles huge payment trafficHow JioHotstar survives the IPL rush
22Real-world · Video at planet scale

How Netflix works

Netflix splits itself in two: a "brain" in the AWS cloud that decides what you can watch and from where, and its own delivery network, placed inside internet providers, that sends the actual video bytes.

325M+paid memberships at the end of 2025
190+countries served
2 planescontrol plane on AWS, data plane on Open Connect
~65Mconcurrent streams at its biggest live event (Nov 2024)
At Ramu's chai stall

Ramu now sells bottled chai all over India. If every bottle had to travel from his Medinipur factory when someone ordered it, deliveries to Chennai would take two days. So every night, while the roads are empty, his trucks pre-stock small fridges inside local kirana shops with the flavours each neighbourhood usually buys. When you order, the app (run from Ramu's head office) checks your account, takes payment, and tells you which nearby shop's fridge to collect from. Head office never touches the bottle itself.

Head office is Netflix's control plane on AWS. The fridges in kirana shops are Open Connect Appliances sitting inside your internet provider. Night-time restocking is the fill window.

Requirements, as an interviewer would set them

Functional
  • Browse, search and get personalised rows
  • Press Play and start within ~2 seconds
  • Smooth playback on any device and network
  • Resume where you stopped, on any device
Non-functional
  • Hundreds of millions of members, evening peaks
  • Video is enormous: bandwidth dominates cost
  • Browsing may degrade; playback must not
  • Survive the loss of a whole cloud region

The big picture: two planes

In plain words

Netflix is two companies glued together: a software company that runs a giant website/app in the cloud, and a "postal service" for video that has put its own post-office boxes inside your internet provider's building. The app decides; the box delivers.

What happens when you press Play

  1. RequestYour app calls the playback API through the Zuul gateway with the title, your device type and its capabilities (codecs, resolution, HDR, DRM type).
  2. ChecksThe playback service confirms your plan allows it (entitlement: number of screens, 4K or not) and prepares a DRM licence so only your device can decrypt the video.
  3. SteeringThe steering service looks at your IP and network, finds which Open Connect appliances near you hold this title in the formats your device supports, checks their health and load, and returns a ranked list of URLs.
  4. StreamThe app downloads the video in small chunks (a few seconds each) straight from the best OCA, choosing a quality for each chunk based on your current bandwidth (adaptive bitrate, below). If one OCA is slow, it switches to the next on the list.
  5. ReportWhile you watch, the app sends events (playing, buffering, quality changes, position) back to the cloud via Kafka-based pipelines. That powers "Continue watching", quality monitoring and recommendations.

Getting the video ready: the encoding pipeline

This is a classic batch, embarrassingly parallel job: split the work into independent pieces, process thousands at once, then stitch. It's the same idea as MapReduce, applied to video.

Adaptive bitrate: why the picture gets blurry instead of freezing

The app keeps a buffer of a few seconds of video ahead of what you're watching. For every next chunk it decides which quality to download. If your bandwidth drops (someone starts a big download, your train enters a tunnel), it switches to a lower quality before the buffer runs dry. A slightly blurry picture is better than a spinning wheel.

LiveAdaptive bitrate player
Network:
—press Play
Buffer (seconds of video ready)

Switch networks while it plays. In adaptive mode the quality follows your bandwidth and the buffer stays healthy. Switch to fixed 1080p and drop to 3G: the buffer drains and playback stalls ("rebuffering"), which is exactly what ABR exists to prevent.

The cloud side: built to survive failure

gateway
Zuul

Every API call enters here: authentication, routing to the right service, rate limiting, canary routing of a slice of traffic to new versions. (Chapter 11)

discovery
Eureka

Services register themselves and find each other by name, not IP, so instances can come and go freely.

resilience
Hystrix → Resilience4j

Netflix popularised circuit breakers and fallbacks: if recommendations fail, show a generic "Trending" row instead of an error page. (Chapter 13)

cache
EVCache

A Memcached-based, replicated cache in front of almost everything; most reads never touch a database. (Chapter 4)

data
Cassandra

Viewing history and other huge, write-heavy, always-available data. An AP choice: a few seconds of staleness in "Continue watching" is fine. (Chapter 8)

events
Kafka pipelines

Trillions of events (plays, pauses, errors) stream to analytics and recommendation systems. (Chapter 9)

testing
Chaos engineering

Chaos Monkey randomly kills production instances during work hours, so teams must build services that shrug it off. Bigger tools fail entire regions on purpose.

regions
Active-active regions

Several AWS regions serve traffic at once; if one degrades, traffic is shifted to the others within minutes.

Recommendations: the reason you keep watching

Most of what members watch is found through recommendations. Heavy models train offline (batch jobs over viewing history), nearline jobs update your profile minutes after you watch something, and an online layer assembles your home page in milliseconds from precomputed results in EVCache. Even the artwork shown for a title is personalised: a romance fan and an action fan may see different thumbnails for the same film.

Real-world lesson: live is different

Netflix's whole delivery model is built on predicting demand and pre-positioning files overnight. Live events break that model: the content doesn't exist until the second it happens, and everyone wants the same seconds at once. During the Jake Paul vs Mike Tyson fight in November 2024 (around 65 million concurrent streams), many viewers saw buffering and errors. Live needs the techniques from the JioHotstar chapter (Chapter 25): massive pre-scaling, short cacheable segments and graceful degradation.

What to take into your own designs

Netflix ideaGeneral principleWhere you learned it
Control plane vs data planeSeparate "deciding" traffic from "heavy bytes" traffic and scale them differentlyChapter 15 (object storage + CDN)
Open Connect inside ISPsMove data close to users; pre-position predictable contentChapter 4
Adaptive bitrateGraceful degradation: lower quality beats total failureChapter 13
Parallel encodingSplit big batch work into independent chunksChapter 15 (batch processing)
Fallback rows, chaos testingExpect failure; design every dependency with a fallbackChapter 13
Lock it in

The brain is in the cloud; the bytes are in the neighbourhood.

Control plane (AWS): login, browse, recommend, decide which server. Data plane (Open Connect): video chunks from inside your ISP, filled overnight. The player adapts quality chunk by chunk so the video keeps playing.

Interview questions

"Design Netflix." Where do you start?

Clarify scope (browse + play, not billing). Split into control plane and data plane immediately: video bandwidth dwarfs everything else, so the core decision is a CDN strategy (pre-positioned caches near users), encoding into an ABR ladder, and a playback API that returns signed URLs to the best nearby servers. Then cover metadata (titles in a cached DB), user data (watch history in Cassandra), recommendations (offline + online), and resilience (fallbacks, multi-region).

Why doesn't Netflix just use a commercial CDN?

At its volume, owning the delivery network is cheaper and gives control over hardware, placement and software. Placing appliances inside ISPs also helps the ISPs (less traffic over their expensive upstream links), so they host the boxes for free. Smaller companies should simply use CloudFront, Akamai or Cloudflare.

How would you store "Continue watching" for 300M users?

A wide-column store like Cassandra partitioned by profile ID, with rows per title holding the last position and timestamp. Writes come every few seconds during playback, so it must be write-optimised and highly available; eventual consistency across regions is acceptable. Cache the top rows of each profile's home page.

Sources: Netflix Q4 2025 shareholder letter (via ComingSoon), the Netflix Tech Blog and Open Connect documentation. Concurrent-stream figure as reported by Netflix for the November 2024 live fight.

Next: How UPI works and scales →
23Real-world · Payments for a billion people

How UPI works and scales

UPI is a central switch (run by NPCI) that every bank and every payments app plugs into. A simple address like ramu@okaxis hides the bank account, and a carefully designed message flow moves money in seconds.

24.51 bnUPI transactions in August 2026, a monthly record
₹29.82 L crvalue moved that month (₹29.82 lakh crore)
~791 M/dayaverage daily transactions
~9,000/saverage per second; evening peaks run several times higher
At Ramu's chai stall

Imagine every customer's bank needing a private phone line to every shop's bank before money could move. With 600+ banks, that's hundreds of thousands of lines, and each bank must trust and test every other bank. Instead, India built one telephone exchange that every bank calls. A customer scans the QR code on Ramu's counter, which says only ramu@okaxis. The exchange looks up which bank and account that is, asks the customer's bank to take ₹15 out, asks Ramu's bank to put ₹15 in, and tells both sides it's done. Ramu's soundbox says "₹15 received" a couple of seconds later.

The exchange is the NPCI UPI switch. ramu@okaxis is a VPA (Virtual Payment Address, now usually called a UPI ID).

The cast

you
Payer and payer's app

PhonePe, Google Pay, Paytm, BHIM or your bank's app. A third-party app works through a "sponsor" PSP bank.

PSP
Payment Service Provider bank

The bank that connects an app to UPI, issues UPI IDs (@okaxis, @ybl) and talks to NPCI on the app's behalf.

switch
NPCI UPI switch

The central hub: routes every message, resolves addresses, enforces rules and timeouts, and keeps the master record of each transaction.

remitter
Payer's bank (issuer)

Holds the payer's account, verifies the UPI PIN, and debits the money.

beneficiary
Payee's bank (acquirer)

Holds the receiver's account and credits the money.

settlement
RBI settlement

Banks don't move real money per transaction. NPCI nets everything and banks settle in batches through their RBI accounts several times a day.

Why a central switch: hub and spoke

In plain words

A UPI ID works like a website name. You type google.com, not an IP address; DNS finds the address. You pay ramu@okaxis, not an account number and IFSC; the switch finds the account. Ramu can change banks without reprinting his QR code if he moves the ID. This layer of indirection is one of the most useful tricks in system design (Chapter 1).

Following one payment, step by step

LiveA ₹250 UPI payment, message by message
  1. StartPriya scans Ramu's QR (upi://pay?pa=ramu@okaxis&am=250) in her app. The app creates a unique transaction ID.
  2. Enter UPI PINThe PIN is typed into NPCI's secure library inside the app and encrypted with keys only the bank can use. Neither PhonePe nor Google Pay ever sees it.
  3. Resolve the addressThe payer's PSP sends the request to NPCI, which asks Ramu's PSP to turn ramu@okaxis into a real account.
  4. DebitNPCI sends a debit request to Priya's bank, which verifies the PIN and device and takes ₹250 out.
  5. CreditNPCI sends a credit request to Ramu's bank, which puts ₹250 in.
  6. ConfirmNPCI marks the transaction successful and notifies both sides. Priya sees the tick; Ramu's soundbox speaks.

When something goes wrong in the middle

The hardest case: Priya's bank debited the money, but Ramu's bank doesn't answer in time. Money has left one account and might or might not have reached the other. UPI's design handles it with patterns you know:

Unique transaction IDs

Every message carries the same ID and reference number, so retries and status checks are idempotent: asking twice never moves money twice. (Chapter 10)

Strict timeouts

NPCI caps how long each step may take. A hung bank doesn't hang the whole network. (Chapter 13)

"Pending" is a real state

The app shows "pending" instead of guessing. The transaction is a state machine: initiated → debited → credited / pending → success / reversed. (Chapter 36)

Check status, then reverse

After a wait, the system asks for the final status; if the credit never happened, the debit is automatically reversed. That's a compensating action, exactly like a saga. (Chapter 14)

Real-world lesson: the retry storm of 2025

In April 2025, UPI suffered a major outage. NPCI found that some banks and payment apps were calling the "check transaction status" API far too often and at very high rates, so the switch's queues overflowed and genuine payments slowed down and failed. The fix, in a circular dated 21 May 2025 (compliance by 31 July 2025), was classic rate limiting (Chapter 12):

  • The first status check may only be sent 90 seconds after the original transaction.
  • Balance enquiries capped at 50 per app, per customer, per day; "list accounts" at 25.
  • Background jobs (autopay mandate execution, merchant list syncs) moved to non-peak hours; peak hours are 10 AM to 1 PM and 5 PM to 9:30 PM.
  • Members that don't comply risk API restrictions or a freeze on onboarding new customers.

The lesson: retries without backoff and limits turn a small slowdown into an outage.

How UPI stays secure

Device binding

On setup, the app sends an SMS from your SIM to prove the phone number is really in this device. Your UPI profile is tied to that device + SIM.

Two factors

Something you have (the bound device) + something you know (UPI PIN). Both are checked on every payment.

PIN never leaves encrypted

NPCI's common library encrypts the PIN on the phone; only the issuing bank can verify it. Apps and PSPs handle only ciphertext.

Limits and risk checks

Per-transaction and daily limits, cooling periods for new devices, and fraud scoring at banks and the switch.

How it scales to billions of transactions a month

Horizontal scale everywhere

App backends, PSP gateways and the switch itself are fleets of stateless nodes behind load balancers. (Chapter 2)

Active-active data centres

The switch runs across data centres at once, so losing one doesn't stop payments. (Chapter 13)

Asynchronous settlement

Real money between banks moves in net batches, not per payment: the fast path only updates ledgers. (Chapter 9)

Tight response times

NPCI shortened its response-time limits for key APIs in 2025, so slow members fail fast instead of holding everyone up.

Protecting the hub

Per-member API rate limits and peak-hour rules stop one misbehaving bank or app from hurting everyone. (Chapter 12)

Concentration limits

A proposed 30% cap on any one app's share of UPI volume (deferred to 31 December 2026) is about systemic risk: no single app should be a single point of failure for the country.

Lock it in

One exchange, a name instead of a number, and "pending" is an honest answer.

Hub and spoke for interoperability, VPA indirection like DNS, idempotent IDs + timeouts + reversal for in-flight failures, and rate limits with backoff so retries can't take the network down.

Interview questions

Design a UPI-like payment system. What are the critical properties?

Exactly-once money movement (idempotent transaction IDs, unique constraints), strong consistency for balances (CP: the debit and credit must reconcile), strict timeouts and an explicit pending state, automatic reversal for failed credits, a full audit trail, security (device binding, 2FA, encryption end to end), and protection of the central switch (rate limits, backpressure, active-active deployment). Settlement can be asynchronous and batched.

Money left my account but the payment shows "failed". What happened, technically?

The debit succeeded at the remitter bank, but the credit leg failed or timed out. The transaction is then reconciled: after status checks confirm the credit didn't happen, the switch triggers a reversal to the remitter bank. Until reconciliation completes, it can look "failed" in the app while the money is in transit back.

Why doesn't UPI just retry the credit forever?

Unbounded retries hold resources and can amplify load on an already struggling bank. A bounded number of checks with backoff, followed by a deterministic outcome (success or reversal) and end-of-day reconciliation, keeps the system stable and the customer informed.

Sources: StartupTalky on NPCI data for August 2026; Inc42 on NPCI's May 2025 API guidelines; IMPRI on NPCI's operational limits. The per-second average is derived from the daily figure.

Next: How Stripe handles huge payment traffic →
24Real-world · Correctness at scale

How Stripe handles huge payment traffic

Stripe's problem isn't only volume; it's that every request moves real money. Its design is built around never charging twice, never losing a payment, and shedding the right traffic when overloaded.

$40 bn+processed from Black Friday to Cyber Monday 2025
578 Mtransactions over that weekend
152,000+transactions per minute at peak (~2,500 every second)
99.9999%+API uptime over that weekend
5 M+database queries per second on its DocDB platform
At Ramu's chai stall

A hotel manager phones Ramu: "Send 500 cups for the conference, charge our account." The line crackles and drops. Did Ramu hear the order? The manager calls again: "Send 500 cups…". If Ramu simply obeys, the hotel gets 1,000 cups and a double bill. So Ramu asks every caller for an order reference: "Is this order H-77? Already noted, here's the same confirmation." Now calling twice is safe.

That reference is Stripe's idempotency key, the most important idea in payment API design.

Requirements

Correctness first
  • Never charge a customer twice
  • Never lose a successful payment
  • Every cent accounted for in a ledger
Always on
  • Merchants lose sales every second Stripe is down
  • Peak events: Black Friday, flash sales, ticket drops
  • Degrade low-value traffic before payments
Developer-friendly
  • Simple, stable REST API
  • Old integrations keep working for years
  • Events delivered to merchants by webhooks

The request path

Idempotency keys: retries without double charges

Networks fail after the server has done the work but before the client hears back. The client can't tell "never arrived" from "done, reply lost". So the client sends a unique Idempotency-Key header (a UUID it generates once per purchase) and reuses it on every retry. Stripe stores the first result for that key and replays it for any repeat.

LivePay ₹500 over a flaky network
Client (merchant server)
Stripe: charges created

With the flaky network on, the first response is "lost" and the client retries automatically. Turn the idempotency key off and pay again: the customer is charged twice.

A payment is a state machine

Surviving Black Friday: rate limiters and load shedders

Stripe has described running four layers of protection. The first two limit individual users; the last two protect the whole fleet by dropping less important traffic first.

This is load shedding with priorities: when there isn't enough capacity for everything, decide in advance what to drop. A merchant's dashboard chart can wait; a customer's checkout can't. (Chapter 12, Chapter 13)

Data: thousands of shards, moved without downtime

Stripe's main online database platform, DocDB, is built on MongoDB Community. Applications talk to a fleet of Go database proxies, which look up a chunk metadata service to route each query to the right shard (a replica set with automatic failover). Every change also streams to Kafka and on to object storage.

Shards fill up unevenly, so data must move between them while payments keep flowing. Stripe's Data Movement Platform does it in six steps, the same pattern you'd use for any live resharding (Chapter 7):

  1. RegisterRecord the planned move in the metadata service; build indexes on the target shard.
  2. Bulk importCopy a point-in-time snapshot of the chunk to the target.
  3. ReplicateReplay every write made since the snapshot from the change stream, until the target catches up.
  4. VerifyCompare source and target snapshots for completeness and correctness.
  5. Switch trafficBriefly block writes to that chunk on the source, let replication drain, update the route. The cutover takes under two seconds; requests that fail during it succeed on retry.
  6. Clean upMark the move complete and delete the chunk from the source.

Three more habits worth copying

Webhooks done right

Events are signed (an HMAC header the merchant verifies), retried with exponential backoff for days, and delivered at-least-once and possibly out of order. Merchants must make handlers idempotent by event ID. (Chapter 9)

Dated API versions

Each account is pinned to the API version it started with (versions are dates). Stripe translates responses for old versions, so a 2017 integration keeps working while new accounts get new behaviour. (Chapter 10)

Double-entry ledger

Every movement of money is recorded as balanced debits and credits. If the books don't sum to zero, something is wrong, and it's detectable. (Built in the banking project, Chapter 39.)

What to take into your own designs

Stripe ideaGeneral principleWhere you learned it
Idempotency keysMake every state-changing API safe to retryChapter 10
PaymentIntent statusesModel long, failure-prone workflows as explicit state machinesChapter 36
Priority load sheddingDecide in advance what to drop under overloadChapter 12
Proxy + metadata routingHide sharding behind a routing layer so data can moveChapter 7
Signed, retried webhooksAt-least-once delivery + idempotent consumersChapter 9
Lock it in

Same key, same answer. Shed the chart before the checkout.

Idempotency keys make retries safe, state machines make payments resumable, tiered limiters keep the fleet alive, and a routing layer lets shards move with zero downtime.

Interview questions

How would you implement idempotency keys?

Store (merchant ID, key) with a unique constraint, plus a hash of the request body, a state (started/completed) and the saved response. The first request inserts the row and does the work; duplicates either get the saved response, a 409 if the first is still running, or a 422 if the body differs. Make the side effects themselves idempotent too (pass the key to downstream systems), and expire keys after a retention window such as 24 hours.

Design a payment gateway that never double-charges.

Idempotency keys at the API, unique constraints in the database, a state machine per payment with each transition persisted before the next external call, idempotency references passed to card networks, a reconciliation job comparing your records with bank settlement files, and an append-only double-entry ledger. Prefer "unknown/pending" plus reconciliation over guessing.

What is load shedding and how is it different from rate limiting?

Rate limiting caps what each client may send, whatever the system's state. Load shedding looks at the system's own health (CPU, in-flight requests, queue length) and drops some requests when it's near overload, choosing the least important ones first. Both return errors early instead of letting the whole service slow to a halt.

Sources: Stripe newsroom, BFCM 2025; Stripe engineering blog on DocDB; Stripe's engineering posts on rate limiters and idempotency, and its PaymentIntent API documentation.

Next: How JioHotstar survives the IPL rush →
25Real-world · Live streaming spikes

How JioHotstar survives the IPL rush

Live cricket creates the worst traffic shape in the internet: crores of people arriving within minutes, all wanting the same seconds of video, and leaving and returning together when a wicket falls. You can't react to that; you have to be ready before it happens.

3.4 crorepeak concurrent viewers on JioHotstar, IPL 2025 opening weekend
~6 croreconcurrent users the platform was prepared for in the 2023 Cricket World Cup
1M+/minhow fast viewers can arrive, faster than servers boot
10+ Tbpsvideo bandwidth at the 2019 record (25.3 million concurrent)
At Ramu's chai stall

Ramu's stall is next to the stadium. On match days, nobody comes for hours, then 20,000 people arrive in the 15 minutes before the toss. When the home captain walks out to bat, the crowd doubles. When he's out, half of them rush out for chai at the same moment. If Ramu waits to see the crowd before lighting extra stoves, the stoves are still heating when the crowd is already angry.

So on match days he lights every stove an hour before the toss (pre-warming), keeps a timetable of when crowds come (scheduled scaling), rehearses with fake crowds (load testing), and if things still get out of hand he stops selling samosas and serves only chai (panic mode: drop everything except the core product).

Why live sport is harder than Netflix

Video on demand (Netflix)Live sport (JioHotstar)
When people watchSpread through the eveningEveryone at the same moment
Content availabilityKnown in advance; pre-copied overnightCreated live, seconds before it's watched
Traffic shapeSmooth daily curveCliffs and spikes driven by match events
Tolerance for delayA few seconds of start-up is fineLag behind TV or a friend's phone feels broken
Failure costWatch laterThe moment is gone forever

The live pipeline

The traffic shape, and why autoscaling alone fails

Normal autoscaling watches CPU, notices it's high, and adds servers. That takes minutes: metrics need to be collected, new machines booted, apps started and warmed. Hotstar's engineers have described traffic growing by more than a million users a minute with roughly a 90-second window to react. By the time reactive scaling catches up, the spike has already hit.

LiveAn illustrative IPL match night: demand vs capacity
Strategy:

The blue area is viewers, the line is capacity. Red marks moments when viewers couldn't be served. Try all three strategies: reactive scaling always arrives late; pre-warming covers the known spikes; panic mode switches off non-essential features so each server can carry more viewers during surprises.

The playbook

before the match
Pre-warm and scale on a schedule

Match times are known. Capacity is raised in big steps well before the toss, instead of waiting for CPU alarms. Machine images are fully baked so new servers start fast.

during
Scale on concurrency, not CPU

The signal that predicts load is "how many people are watching and how fast that's growing". Scaling keys off that business metric, in steps (a "ladder").

rehearsal
Load test at full size

For 2019, the "Project Hulk" load tests used about 108,000 CPUs across 8 regions generating around 200 Gbps, including sudden "tsunami" surges and chaos experiments.

emergency
Panic mode: the video must play on

Every service is ranked. Under pressure, non-critical features (recommendations, personalisation, some widgets) are switched off so streaming, login and payments keep their capacity.

edge
Push APIs to the CDN

For 2023, frequently hit but cacheable APIs (scorecards, highlights) moved to a separate CDN domain with lighter rules, and refresh intervals were made longer, cutting origin calls.

clients
Polite clients

Apps retry with backoff and jitter, and push notifications go out in batches so they don't summon everyone in the same second. (Chapter 13)

Wickets and the "tsunami"

Infrastructure lessons from the 2023 World Cup rebuild

Disney+ Hotstar's engineers have written about hitting walls that only appear at this scale. Each is a lesson about hidden single points of contention:

Wall they hitFixGeneral lesson
One NAT gateway per availability zone used 50% of its bandwidth at only 10% of expected loadOne NAT gateway per subnetFind shared chokepoints before the real event, with measurement
Several API gateway pods on one node saturated its network (8–9 Gbps)Bigger network nodes, and topology rules allowing one gateway pod per nodeSpread hot components; CPU isn't the only resource
Hundreds of per-service load balancers to pre-warm by hand; NodePort ports running outA shared Envoy-based gateway layer and direct pod routing (ClusterIP)Centralise cross-cutting concerns (routing, auth, rate limits, load shedding)
Adding 400+ nodes at once throttled the Kubernetes control planeStep-wise scaling, 100–300 nodes per stepEven the scaler has limits; scale in controlled steps
Latency-critical video services competing with heavy ads/personalisation workloadsSeparate clusters per workload type; one critical (P0) stack per cluster for headroomBulkheads at the infrastructure level (Chapter 13)
Lock it in

Light the stoves before the toss. Serve only chai when the crowd overflows.

Spikes faster than boot time need pre-warming and scheduled, step-wise scaling on concurrency. Rehearse with full-size load tests, push everything cacheable to the CDN, and keep a panic mode that sheds non-essential features so the video keeps playing.

Interview questions

Design a live-streaming platform for 5 crore concurrent viewers.

Video: ingest → live transcoding into an ABR ladder → packaging into short HLS/DASH segments → origin with a shield layer → multiple CDNs, with players fetching segments and adapting quality. APIs: stateless services on Kubernetes behind a gateway, cacheable responses on the CDN, sessions and entitlement in fast stores. Scale: pre-warm by schedule, scale on concurrency in steps, keep headroom, priority-based load shedding and feature kill switches. Prove it with full-size load and chaos tests. Clients: retries with jitter, batched notifications.

Why is scaling on CPU a poor fit for live events?

CPU is a lagging signal: it rises only after users arrive, and new capacity takes minutes to become ready, while viewers can arrive at over a million a minute. A leading signal (match schedule, concurrency and its growth rate) lets you scale before the load lands.

What would you switch off first in panic mode, and why?

Anything that isn't on the critical path to watching: personalised recommendations, social features, non-essential widgets, analytics with high fan-out. Keep login, entitlement, playback tokens, video delivery and payments. Decide this ranking before the event, wire kill switches into the services, and rehearse flipping them.

Sources: Social Samosa on IPL 2025 opening weekend; ByteByteGo on Hotstar's 2023 scaling; Hotstar engineering blog; summary of Hotstar's AWS re:Invent 2019 talk. The match in the simulator is illustrative, not real data.

Next: Part 3 · Low-Level Design →

Part 3 · Chapters 26 to 27

Low-Level Design: drawing the rooms

Now we zoom into one service and design its insides: the classes, their responsibilities, and how they connect. Good LLD makes code easy to read, test and change.

The four pillars of OOPUML, relationships, cohesion and coupling
26LLD · Foundations

The four pillars of object-oriented programming

OOP organises code around objects that bundle data with the behaviour that acts on it. Four ideas make that work: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance and polymorphism.

At Ramu's chai stall

Ramu orders automatic chai machines for every branch. A staff member presses "Make Masala Chai"; they never touch the boiler or the valve timings. The machine protects its insides (encapsulation) and offers simple buttons that hide the steps (abstraction). The new "Masala" model is built from the basic model plus a spice dispenser (inheritance). And every model has the same big "Brew" button, but each one brews its own way (polymorphism).

Class vs object

Class = the blueprint

The cookie cutter. Describes what data (fields) and behaviour (methods) every object of this kind has. class ChaiMachine.

Object = a real thing made from it

The actual cookies. Each has its own values. new ChaiMachine("Kolkata-01").

1. Encapsulation: protect your insides

Definition

Bundle data and the methods that operate on it in one unit, and restrict direct access to the data (private fields), exposing only controlled operations that keep it valid.

2. Abstraction: show what, hide how

Definition

Expose only the essential features of something through a simple interface, hiding implementation details. In Java: interfaces and abstract classes.

In plain words

You drive a car with a steering wheel and two pedals. You don't need to know about fuel injection. If the company swaps a petrol engine for an electric one, you still drive the same way. Encapsulation is about protecting the engine; abstraction is about simplifying how you use it.

3. Inheritance: an "is-a" relationship

Definition

A class (child/subclass) acquires the fields and methods of another (parent/superclass) using extends, and can add or override behaviour. Use it only for a true "is-a" relationship.

Common trap

Using inheritance just to reuse code ("Stack extends ArrayList" so I get add() for free). Now a Stack exposes add(index, x), which breaks stack rules. Deep hierarchies also become fragile: a change in a parent ripples to every child. Prefer composition ("has-a") unless it's truly "is-a" (Chapter 33).

4. Polymorphism: one call, many behaviours

compile-time
Overloading

Same method name, different parameters, in one class. The compiler picks: price(Chai c), price(Chai c, Size s).

runtime
Overriding

A child redefines a parent's method. The JVM picks the version based on the actual object at runtime (dynamic dispatch).

Abstract class vs interface

Abstract classInterface
Meaning"Is a kind of" with shared base code"Can do" a capability / contract
State (fields)Yes, instance fieldsOnly constants (static final)
ConstructorsYesNo
Method bodiesYes, anydefault and static methods (Java 8+), private (Java 9+)
How many?A class extends only oneA class implements many
Exampleabstract class Chaiinterface Payable, Comparable, Runnable
Lock it in

"A PIE": Abstraction, Polymorphism, Inheritance, Encapsulation.

Encapsulation protects (private fields + validating methods). Abstraction simplifies (interfaces). Inheritance reuses for "is-a" only. Polymorphism replaces if (type == …) chains with overridden methods.

Interview questions

What's the difference between encapsulation and abstraction?

Encapsulation is about hiding data and protecting an object's internal state (implementation level: private fields, getters, validation). Abstraction is about hiding complexity and exposing only what's needed to use something (design level: interfaces, abstract methods). Encapsulation is how you achieve the information hiding that abstraction promises.

Can you override a static or private method?

No. Private methods aren't visible to subclasses, so a same-named method in a child is a new method. Static methods belong to the class; a same-signature static method in a child hides the parent's (method hiding), and which one runs depends on the reference type at compile time, not the object.

Next: UML, relationships, cohesion and coupling →
27LLD · Foundations

UML class diagrams, relationships, cohesion and coupling

A class diagram is the floor plan of your code. Six kinds of lines describe how classes relate, and two words, cohesion and coupling, describe whether the plan is any good.

At Ramu's chai stall

An order is made of order lines ("2 masala chai"). Tear up the order slip and its lines are gone too: that's composition. A stall has employees, but if the stall closes, Bablu still exists and joins another stall: that's aggregation. A customer places orders; both exist independently: association. The billing clerk borrows a calculator for a moment and gives it back: dependency.

Reading a class box

The six relationships

Multiplicity

1 exactly one · 0..1 optional · * or 0..* any number · 1..* at least one. "A Customer (1) places Orders (0..*)".

Sequence diagrams: who calls whom, in what order

Cohesion and coupling: the two quality dials

Cohesion: how focused is one module?

High cohesion = everything inside a class is about one thing. A TaxCalculator that only calculates tax. Want it high.

Coupling: how tangled are modules?

Low coupling = classes know little about each other and talk through small interfaces. Change one, the others don't care. Want it low.

Every SOLID principle in the next part is, at heart, a technique for raising cohesion and lowering coupling.

Lock it in

Triangle = is-a. Diamond = has-a (filled: dies together). Dashed = uses / implements.

Composition ◆ vs aggregation ◇: does the part die with the whole? And the golden rule of design: high cohesion, low coupling.

Interview questions

Composition vs aggregation: give a real example of each.

Composition: House and Room; destroy the house and its rooms cease to exist; rooms aren't shared. In code, the whole creates and exclusively owns the parts. Aggregation: Team and Player; the team disbands but players continue and may belong to other teams. In code, parts are created elsewhere and passed in.

How do you reduce coupling between two classes?

Depend on an interface instead of a concrete class; inject dependencies rather than creating them with new; expose fewer public methods; communicate via events where a direct call isn't needed; follow the Law of Demeter (don't reach through objects: a.getB().getC().doX()).

Next: Part 4 · SOLID principles →

Part 4 · Chapters 28 to 33

SOLID: the building codes

Five principles, collected by Robert C. Martin ("Uncle Bob"), that keep object-oriented code easy to change. Each one answers the same question: when requirements change, how few places do I have to touch?

S · Single ResponsibilityO · Open/ClosedL · Liskov SubstitutionI · Interface SegregationD · Dependency InversionBeyond SOLID: DRY, KISS, YAGNI, composition
28SOLID · S

Single Responsibility Principle

A class should have one, and only one, reason to change. One job, one owner.

At Ramu's chai stall

Ramu's first employee, Gopal, did everything: brewed tea, took cash, kept the accounts, cleaned up and handled deliveries. One April the GST rules changed. While Gopal was busy redoing the accounts, he forgot the milk on the stove and it boiled over. A change in tax rules broke tea making, two things that had nothing to do with each other except that one person did both.

Ramu hired a cook, a cashier and an accountant. Now a tax change only touches the accountant.

Definition

"A module should be responsible to one, and only one, actor." An actor is a group of people who would ask for changes: the finance team, the marketing team, the DBA. If two different groups can ask you to change the same class for different reasons, it has two responsibilities.

In plain words

A Swiss Army knife is handy, but if the scissors break you have to send the whole knife away, losing the blade too. Separate tools can be fixed, replaced and tested one at a time.

How to spot an SRP violation

The name has "And" or "Manager"

UserAndOrderManager, Utils, Helper.

Unrelated imports

java.sql, javax.mail and a PDF library in one file.

The "describe it" test

You can't say what it does without using "and".

Merge conflicts

Several teams keep editing the same file for different reasons.

Common trap

SRP does not mean "one method per class" or "tiny classes everywhere". A TaxCalculator with ten tax methods is fine: they all change for the same reason. Splitting too far scatters one idea across many files and lowers cohesion.

Lock it in

One cook, one stove. One class, one reason to change.

Ask: "Who would ask me to change this?" If the answer is more than one team, split it. In Spring, the Controller → Service → Repository layering is SRP at the architecture level.

Interview questions

How do you explain SRP to a junior developer?

Group together the things that change for the same reason, and separate the things that change for different reasons. If the tax team, the email team and the database team could each ask you to edit the same class, that class is doing three jobs and a change for one can break the others.

Does a Spring @RestController that validates input, calls a service and maps the response violate SRP?

Not necessarily. Its single responsibility is HTTP adaptation: turning requests into service calls and results into responses. Bean validation annotations and a mapper keep it thin. It violates SRP when business rules, SQL or transaction logic creep into the controller.

Next: O · Open/Closed →
29SOLID · O

Open/Closed Principle

Software should be open for extension but closed for modification. Add new behaviour by adding new code, not by editing code that already works.

At Ramu's chai stall

Ramu's first menu was painted directly on the wall. Every time he added a drink (cold coffee in summer, kadha in winter) a painter had to repaint the wall, and twice he smudged existing prices. So Ramu switched to a board with slots: each item is a card that slides in. The board itself never changes; it's closed. But it's open: any number of new cards can be added.

Definition

A module should allow its behaviour to be extended without changing its source code. In Java you achieve it with abstractions (interfaces / abstract classes) plus polymorphism: the stable code depends on the interface, and new behaviour arrives as new implementations.

Interview tip

OCP is what the Strategy, Decorator, Template Method and Observer patterns are for. When you see a growing switch or if-else on a type, say: "I'd replace this conditional with polymorphism so new types are additions, not edits."

Common trap

Making everything pluggable "just in case". OCP is applied where change is likely (pricing rules, payment methods, notification channels). Abstracting things that never vary adds indirection for nothing (see YAGNI, Chapter 33).

Lock it in

Slide in a new card; don't repaint the wall.

Stable code depends on an interface; new behaviour = new class. A growing switch on type is the classic OCP smell.

Interview questions

Where does the JDK or Spring itself follow OCP?

Collections.sort(list, comparator): the sort algorithm is closed, and you extend the ordering with any Comparator. In Spring: add a HandlerInterceptor, a Filter, a new @Bean implementing an interface, or a BeanPostProcessor, and the framework picks it up without its code changing.

Is it ever OK to modify existing code?

Of course: to fix bugs, and to refactor towards an abstraction the first time a second variant appears ("rule of three"). OCP is a goal for the parts of the system that change for predictable reasons, not a ban on editing.

Next: L · Liskov Substitution →
30SOLID · L

Liskov Substitution Principle

If B is a subtype of A, you must be able to use a B anywhere an A is expected, without surprises. A child class must keep its parent's promises.

At Ramu's chai stall

Ramu's delivery boy Raju falls sick, and the agency sends a replacement: "He's a delivery boy too." Ramu hands him 20 orders and the scooter keys. Turns out the replacement can't ride a scooter; he only walks. Every delivery is 40 minutes late. On paper he is a delivery boy, but he can't be substituted for one, because he breaks the promise everyone relied on: "deliveries arrive within 15 minutes".

Definition

Barbara Liskov (1987): objects of a superclass should be replaceable with objects of its subclasses without altering the correctness of the program. In practice a subclass must not:

  • Demand more (stronger preconditions): parent accepts any amount, child rejects amounts over ₹100.
  • Promise less (weaker postconditions): parent always returns a receipt, child sometimes returns null.
  • Break invariants: rules that must always hold for the parent (balance ≥ 0).
  • Throw new surprises: UnsupportedOperationException for an inherited method.

The famous one: is a Square a Rectangle?

Signs you're breaking LSP

Empty or throwing overrides

throw new UnsupportedOperationException() in a subclass.

instanceof checks

Callers test the concrete type before calling a parent method.

"Is-a" in English only

Penguin is a bird, but Bird.fly() doesn't fit it.

Even the JDK bends this rule: List.of(…) and Collections.unmodifiableList(…) are Lists whose add() throws UnsupportedOperationException. A good interview talking point.

Lock it in

If it looks like a duck but needs batteries, it's the wrong abstraction.

A subtype must accept at least as much, deliver at least as much, and never surprise. Inheritance means "behaves like", not just "is called".

Interview questions

How is LSP related to OCP?

OCP relies on swapping implementations behind an abstraction. That only works if every implementation honours the abstraction's contract, which is exactly what LSP guarantees. An LSP violation forces instanceof checks into the calling code, which then has to be modified for each new subtype, breaking OCP.

How would you fix Bird / Penguin?

Remove fly() from Bird. Keep common behaviour (eat(), layEggs()) in Bird, and add a Flyable interface implemented only by birds that fly. Code that needs flying takes Flyable.

Next: I · Interface Segregation →
31SOLID · I

Interface Segregation Principle

No client should be forced to depend on methods it doesn't use. Many small, focused interfaces beat one fat one.

At Ramu's chai stall

Ramu's hiring form had one job description for everyone: "Must brew tea, drive the delivery van, and maintain the accounts ledger." The cook can't drive, the driver can't do accounts, and the accountant can't make tea, so every new hire had to fake two-thirds of the job. Ramu replaced it with three short role cards: Brewer, Driver, Accountant. His nephew, who can brew and drive, simply holds two cards.

Definition

Split large interfaces into smaller, role-specific ones so that implementers only implement what they can genuinely do, and callers only depend on what they genuinely use. SRP applied to interfaces.

Interview tip

Spring Data shows ISP in layers: Repository (marker) → CrudRepository → PagingAndSortingRepository → JpaRepository. You can also declare a tiny custom interface extending Repository<Order, Long> with only findById and save, so the service can't call deleteAll() by mistake.

Lock it in

Role cards, not one giant job description.

If an implementer throws UnsupportedOperationException or leaves methods empty, the interface is too fat. Split by who uses it.

Interview questions

Doesn't ISP lead to too many interfaces?

It can if applied blindly. Split along real client needs: if every client uses all methods together, one interface is right. Split when distinct groups of clients use distinct subsets, or when some implementers can't support some methods.

Next: D · Dependency Inversion →
32SOLID · D

Dependency Inversion Principle

High-level policy should not depend on low-level details. Both should depend on abstractions. Plug into a socket, don't wire into the wall.

At Ramu's chai stall

The flagship stall's stove was welded straight onto one company's gas pipe. When that supplier tripled prices, switching meant breaking the wall. So Ramu had the electrician fit a standard socket. Now gas stove, induction plate or electric kettle, anything with the standard plug works. The kitchen (high-level) depends on the socket standard (abstraction), and so does every appliance (low-level). Neither depends directly on the other.

Definition

1. High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules; both should depend on abstractions. 2. Abstractions should not depend on details; details should depend on abstractions. The abstraction is owned by the high-level side, which is why the dependency arrow is "inverted".

DIP, DI and IoC are three different things

TermWhat it isExample
Dependency Inversion PrincipleA design principle: depend on abstractions, with the abstraction owned by the high-level moduleOrderService depends on OrderRepository interface
Dependency InjectionA technique: give an object its dependencies from outside (constructor, setter, field)new OrderService(repo, notifier)
Inversion of ControlA broader idea: the framework controls object creation and the flow, calling your codeSpring's ApplicationContext creates beans and wires them

Prefer constructor injection: dependencies are explicit, fields can be final, objects are never half-built, and tests can use plain new. Field injection with @Autowired hides dependencies and needs reflection in tests.

Lock it in

Plug into a socket, don't weld to the pipe.

Business code depends on interfaces it owns; databases, email, HTTP clients are plugins. If you see new SomeConcreteService() inside business logic, you've found a DIP violation.

Interview questions

Why is it called "inversion"?

In a naive layered design, the source-code dependency follows the call direction: business → database. With DIP, the business layer defines the interface and the database layer implements it, so the source-code dependency points from the database layer up to the business layer, opposite to the flow of control. The dependency has been inverted.

With two implementations of an interface, how does Spring choose one?

It fails with NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException unless you disambiguate: mark one @Primary, use @Qualifier("sms") at the injection point, inject List<Notifier> or Map<String, Notifier> to get all, or activate one with @Profile / @ConditionalOnProperty.

Next: Beyond SOLID: DRY, KISS, YAGNI, composition →
33Design principles

Beyond SOLID: DRY, KISS, YAGNI, composition and Demeter

A handful of short rules that every reviewer will quote at you. Know each one, its meaning, and when it's misused.

DRY
Don't Repeat Yourself

Every piece of knowledge (a rule, a formula) should live in one place. GST rate in five files = five bugs waiting. But don't merge code that only looks alike yet changes for different reasons.

KISS
Keep It Simple, Stupid

The simplest design that works is usually best. A for loop beats a clever 4-level stream pipeline nobody can read.

YAGNI
You Aren't Gonna Need It

Don't build features or abstractions for imagined futures. Build them when the need is real.

SoC
Separation of Concerns

Keep UI, business logic and data access in separate layers.

TDA
Tell, Don't Ask

Tell an object to do something instead of pulling its data out and deciding for it: wallet.withdraw(x), not if (wallet.getBalance() >= x) wallet.setBalance(…).

Fail fast
Fail fast

Validate early and throw clear errors at the boundary, instead of letting bad data travel deep into the system.

Composition over inheritance

At Ramu's chai stall

Ramu's nephew designed menu classes by inheritance: Chai, GingerChai, GingerElaichiChai, GingerElaichiSugarFreeChai, IcedGingerElaichiSugarFreeChai… Thirty classes later, every new flavour doubled the count. The fix: one Chai that has a list of add-ons. Build any combination at runtime.

Law of Demeter: talk only to your friends

A method should only call methods on: itself, its fields, its parameters, and objects it creates. Not on objects returned by those ("don't talk to strangers").

SOLID on one page

LetterPrincipleOne lineChai pictureSmell
SSingle ResponsibilityOne reason to changeCook, cashier, accountantGod class, "Manager", "And"
OOpen/ClosedExtend by adding, not editingSlot menu boardGrowing switch on type
LLiskov SubstitutionSubtypes keep the parent's promisesDelivery boy who can't rideUnsupportedOperationException, instanceof
IInterface SegregationSmall, role-based interfacesRole cardsEmpty / throwing implementations
DDependency InversionDepend on abstractions you ownStandard socketnew Concrete() in business code
Lock it in

"Some Old Lions Instantly Dance": S·O·L·I·D

Plus: DRY the knowledge, KISS the code, YAGNI the speculation, compose rather than inherit, and don't talk to strangers.

Interview questions

When does DRY go wrong?

When two pieces of code look the same by coincidence but represent different knowledge. Merging them into one shared function couples two features; when one changes, you add flags and ifs to the shared code until it's worse than the duplication. "Duplication is far cheaper than the wrong abstraction." (Sandi Metz)

Can SOLID principles conflict with KISS or YAGNI?

Yes. Over-applying SOLID creates interfaces with one implementation, factories for everything and deep indirection. Apply SOLID where change is expected or testing needs it; keep the rest simple. Principles are tools for managing change, not goals in themselves.

Next: Part 5 · Design patterns →

Part 5 · Chapters 34 to 37

Design patterns: the recipe book

Patterns are named, proven solutions to problems that keep coming back. Knowing them gives you ready-made designs and a shared vocabulary: say "use a Strategy here" and every engineer knows what you mean.

Creational patternsStructural patternsBehavioral patternsConcurrency in LLD
34Patterns · Creational

Creational patterns: how objects get made

Creational patterns control object creation so that code isn't littered with new and complicated construction logic.

Singleton: exactly one instance

At Ramu's chai stall

There is one master cash register for the whole shop. If every cashier bought their own register, the day's totals would never add up. Everyone uses the register.

Intent: ensure a class has only one instance and provide a global access point. Use for: configuration, a connection pool, a registry, a logger. Real world: Runtime.getRuntime(); Spring beans are singletons per container by default.

Common trap

Singletons are global state in disguise: they hide dependencies and make tests share state. In Spring apps, let the container manage a single bean and inject it instead of calling getInstance() everywhere.

Factory (Simple Factory and Factory Method): hide which class gets built

At Ramu's chai stall

A customer says "One lemon tea." They don't go into the kitchen and pick a machine. The counter (the factory) decides which machine makes it and hands over the cup.

Intent: create objects without the caller knowing the concrete class. Factory Method (GoF) lets subclasses decide which class to instantiate; the everyday simple factory is one method with the decision inside. Real world: Calendar.getInstance(), NumberFormat.getInstance(), Spring BeanFactory.

Abstract Factory: families of things that belong together

Intent: create families of related objects without naming their concrete classes, so the pieces always match. The Kolkata branch kit gives a clay kulhad cup and a samosa; the Mumbai kit gives a glass cutting-chai cup and vada pav. You never mix a kulhad with vada pav.

Builder: construct complex objects step by step

At Ramu's chai stall

A catering order has 15 options: cups, flavour, sugar level, milk type, delivery time, address, cups or flasks, invoice name… Shouting them all in one breath in a fixed order is a recipe for mistakes. A form you fill field by field, then submit, is a builder.

Prototype: copy a ready-made object

Intent: create new objects by copying an existing, configured one instead of building from scratch. Ramu keeps a "standard wedding package" template; for each new wedding he copies it and changes the date and address.

Lock it in

"Sita Found A Big Present": Singleton, Factory, Abstract factory, Builder, Prototype.

Singleton = one. Factory = which one. Abstract factory = matching set. Builder = many options, step by step. Prototype = copy and tweak.

Interview questions

How can a singleton be broken, and how does an enum prevent it?

Reflection can call the private constructor; serialization/deserialization creates a new instance (unless readResolve is defined); cloning can copy it; and multiple class loaders each get their own. Enums are protected by the JVM: their constructors can't be invoked reflectively and serialization returns the same constant.

Factory Method vs Abstract Factory?

Factory Method creates one product, and subclasses decide its class by overriding a method (inheritance). Abstract Factory creates a family of related products through an object you pass in (composition). An abstract factory is often implemented with several factory methods.

Next: Structural patterns →
35Patterns · Structural

Structural patterns: how objects fit together

Structural patterns combine classes and objects into bigger structures while keeping them flexible: wrapping, adapting, simplifying and nesting.

Adapter: make incompatible interfaces work together

At Ramu's chai stall

The new UPI card machine has a USB-C cable; the old billing computer only has USB-A. Ramu doesn't replace either: he buys a small adapter dongle.

Decorator: add behaviour by wrapping

Facade: one simple front for a complicated system

Ramu's mobile app has a single "Order again" button. Behind it: check stock, reserve it, charge the saved card, tell the kitchen, book a rider. The button is a facade.

Proxy: a stand-in that controls access

A proxy has the same interface as the real object and sits in front of it to add control: caching, lazy loading, access checks, remote calls, transactions.

Virtual proxy

Delay creating something expensive (Hibernate lazy-loaded collections).

Protection proxy

Check permissions before calling (Spring Security @PreAuthorize).

Remote proxy

Local object that forwards calls over the network (gRPC stubs, Feign clients).

Caching / smart proxy

Return cached results, count calls, open transactions (Spring @Transactional, @Cacheable).

Decorator vs Proxy: same shape, different intent. A decorator adds features and is usually stacked by the client; a proxy controls access to one subject and is usually invisible to the client.

Composite: treat a group like a single item

The menu has items (Masala chai ₹15) and categories that contain items or other categories ("Combos" → "Breakfast combo" → chai + samosa). You want price() to work on any of them.

Bridge and Flyweight, briefly

Bridge
Split two dimensions that vary independently

Messages (OrderAlert, PromoMessage) × channels (SMS, Email). Instead of 2×2 subclasses, a Message has a Channel. Add a channel or a message type independently. JDBC: the DriverManager/API side and the vendor driver side are a bridge.

Flyweight
Share common state to save memory

Millions of map markers share one icon image object; only position differs. JDK: Integer.valueOf(-128..127) cache, the String pool.

Lock it in

Adapter converts, Decorator adds, Facade simplifies, Proxy guards, Composite nests, Bridge splits.

Adapter = different interface → mine. Decorator = same interface + extra. Proxy = same interface + control. Facade = new, simpler interface over many.

Interview questions

Adapter vs Facade?

Adapter makes one existing interface match another interface that clients already expect; it's about compatibility. Facade defines a new, simpler interface over a whole subsystem; it's about convenience. An adapter usually wraps one object; a facade usually coordinates many.

Where are decorators used in the JDK?

java.io: BufferedInputStream, DataInputStream, GZIPInputStream all wrap another InputStream. Also Collections.synchronizedList() and Collections.unmodifiableList() wrap a list to add synchronization or read-only behaviour.

Next: Behavioral patterns →
36Patterns · Behavioral

Behavioral patterns: how objects cooperate

Behavioral patterns are about responsibilities and communication: who decides, who gets told, and how work passes along.

Strategy: swap the algorithm

At Ramu's chai stall

Delivery charges change with the situation: normal days ₹20, rainy days surge pricing, festival days free over ₹200. The delivery desk keeps a card for each pricing rule and simply picks today's card.

Observer: tell everyone who cares

At Ramu's chai stall

When a fresh batch of samosas comes out, Ramu rings a bell. Whoever is waiting (customers, the delivery desk, the stock clerk) reacts in their own way. Ramu doesn't need to know who's listening.

Command: turn a request into an object

An order slip is a request written down: it can be queued, logged, retried, or cancelled (undone). The Command pattern does the same in code.

State: behaviour changes with state

Template Method: fixed steps, customisable details

You met this in Chapter 26: Chai.prepare() is final and fixes the order of steps; subclasses fill in addExtras(). Real world: Spring's JdbcTemplate, RestTemplate, AbstractController; JUnit's setUp/test/tearDown lifecycle; HttpServlet.service() calling doGet()/doPost().

Chain of Responsibility: pass it along until someone handles it

At Ramu's chai stall

Refunds: the cashier can approve up to ₹100, the branch manager up to ₹1,000, anything bigger goes to Ramu. A request walks up the chain until someone has the authority.

Four more to recognise

Iterator
Walk a collection without exposing its insides

Iterator<T>, the for-each loop. Lists, sets and trees all iterate the same way.

Mediator
A central hub so objects don't talk directly

An airport control tower; a chat room routing messages between users. Cuts many-to-many links to one-to-many.

Memento
Save and restore an object's state

"Undo" in an editor; saving a game checkpoint, without exposing internals.

Visitor
Add operations to a class hierarchy without editing it

Tax calculation and export over a tree of menu items; compilers walking syntax trees.

Which pattern solves which problem?

When you see…Reach for
A big if/switch choosing an algorithmStrategy
A big switch on status in many methodsState
"When X happens, also do Y, Z…"Observer / events
Constructors with many parametersBuilder
new ConcreteClass() decided by input, repeated around the codeFactory
Adding optional features in layersDecorator
Third-party API doesn't fit your interfaceAdapter
Callers need one easy entry to many subsystemsFacade
Need caching, lazy loading or access checks transparentlyProxy
Tree of things, treated uniformlyComposite
Requests that need queuing, logging or undoCommand
Several possible handlers, in orderChain of Responsibility
Same skeleton, different stepsTemplate Method
Lock it in

Strategy swaps HOW. State swaps WHO-I-AM. Observer shouts WHAT-HAPPENED.

Command = request as an object (queue, undo). Template = fixed recipe, custom steps. Chain = pass it up until someone handles it.

Interview questions

Strategy vs State: they look identical. What's the difference?

Structurally both delegate to an interface. In Strategy, the client picks the algorithm and strategies don't know about each other. In State, the state objects themselves trigger transitions to the next state, and the set of allowed operations changes as the object moves through its lifecycle.

What's the downside of the Observer pattern?

Flow becomes implicit: reading the publisher doesn't tell you what happens next. Listener order may be undefined, a slow or failing listener can affect the publisher if run synchronously, and forgotten subscriptions leak memory. Use clear event names, async listeners for slow work, and tracing.

Next: Concurrency in LLD →
37LLD · Correctness

Concurrency in LLD: when two people grab the last samosa

Many LLD questions (booking seats, parking spots, wallets) are really about concurrency. Interviewers want to see you protect shared state.

At Ramu's chai stall

One samosa left. Two cashiers each check the tray ("yes, one left"), each take money from a customer, each walk to the tray. One customer gets a samosa; the other gets an apology. Checking and taking were two separate steps, and someone squeezed in between. That's a race condition.

ToolUse forNote
synchronizedSimple mutual exclusion on an objectEasy; one lock per object; no timeout
ReentrantLockTry-lock with timeout, fairness, multiple conditionsAlways unlock in finally
ReadWriteLockMany readers, few writers (a menu cache)Readers don't block each other
AtomicInteger/Long, LongAdderCounters (cups sold, IDs)Lock-free compare-and-swap
ConcurrentHashMapShared maps; compute, putIfAbsentNever use plain HashMap across threads
BlockingQueueProducer–consumer (order slips to cooks)put() waits when full, take() waits when empty
Immutable objectsValue objects (Money, Address, records)No shared mutable state = no races
Lock it in

Check-then-act must be one step.

In one JVM: atomic operations, concurrent collections, locks. Across servers: DB conditional updates, unique constraints, optimistic versions, or Redis SET NX. Prefer immutability where you can.

Next: Part 6 · LLD projects →

Part 6 · Chapters 38 to 40

LLD projects: build the whole thing

Three complete low-level designs, each with requirements, a class diagram, working Java and the follow-up questions interviewers ask. Every principle and pattern from the last three parts shows up here, used for a reason.

LLD project: parking lotLLD project: banking systemLLD project: multi-level IAM and auth
38LLD · Project

LLD project: a parking lot

The most common LLD interview question, solved with the framework, a class diagram and working, thread-safe Java that uses the principles and patterns from this book.

The LLD interview framework

  1. Clarify requirements (5 min)What must it do? What's out of scope? Ask about scale, concurrency and which parts may change in future.
  2. Find the entities (5 min)Underline the nouns in the requirements: they become classes. Verbs become methods.
  3. Draw the class diagram (10 min)Classes, key fields and methods, relationships and multiplicities. Mark interfaces where things vary.
  4. Pick patterns where they fit (in passing)Strategy for rules that vary, State for lifecycles, Observer for notifications, Factory for creation. Say why.
  5. Write the core code (20 min)The main flows end to end, clean names, SOLID. Skip boilerplate (getters, imports).
  6. Discuss concurrency, edge cases, extensions (5 min)Two cars, one spot. Lost tickets. A new vehicle type. Show that adding it is an addition, not a rewrite.

Step 1 · Requirements

Must have
  • Several floors, each with spots of sizes SMALL, MEDIUM, LARGE
  • Bikes, cars, trucks; a vehicle may use a bigger spot if its size is full
  • Entry: assign a spot, issue a ticket
  • Exit: compute fee by duration and vehicle type, take payment, free the spot
  • Show free spots per floor
Design goals
  • Two entry gates must never assign the same spot
  • Pricing rules and allocation rules will change (weekend rates, EV-first floors)
  • Easy to add a vehicle type (EV, bus)
  • Out of scope: reservations, licence plate cameras

Steps 2–3 · Entities and class diagram

Step 5 · The code

Step 6 · How the design answers follow-up questions

Interviewer asksAnswerPrinciple / pattern
"Two cars arrive at two gates for the last spot."tryOccupy is a compare-and-set; exactly one wins, the other's strategy moves to the next spotAtomic check-then-act
"Add weekend pricing."New WeekendPricing implements PricingStrategy; inject it. No existing class editedStrategy, OCP

Lock it in

Nouns → classes, verbs → methods, "what changes?" → interfaces.

Every LLD answer should show: clear entities, composition over inheritance, Strategy/State where rules vary, atomic handling of shared resources, and an extension that needs no edits.

Next: LLD project: banking system →
39LLD · Project

LLD project: a banking system

Accounts, deposits, withdrawals and transfers that are correct under concurrency, auditable to the paisa, and safe to retry. The favourite LLD question for fintech and payments interviews.

At Ramu's chai stall

Ramu's chain now runs a small staff savings scheme. Two cashiers, at the same second, process "Bablu sends ₹500 to Gopal" and "Gopal sends ₹200 to Bablu". Each cashier grabs one passbook and waits for the other's. Neither lets go. The queue stops. That's a deadlock. Ramu's rule from then on: always pick up the passbook with the smaller account number first. Nobody can ever end up holding one while waiting for the other in a circle.

Step 1 · Requirements

Functional
  • Customers open savings, current and fixed-deposit accounts
  • Deposit, withdraw, transfer between accounts
  • Statement: full history of every movement
  • Account states: active, frozen, closed
  • Monthly interest for savings accounts
  • SMS/email alert on every debit
Rules and guarantees
  • Balance never goes below zero (or below the overdraft limit for current accounts)
  • Daily withdrawal/transfer limit per account
  • A retried transfer never moves money twice
  • Concurrent transfers never deadlock or lose updates
  • Money is never created or destroyed: every debit has a matching credit

Step 2 · Key design decisions

value object
Money, not double

BigDecimal with currency, immutable. 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3 in floating point; banks can't round randomly.

audit
Double-entry ledger

Every transfer writes two ledger entries (debit A, credit B) that sum to zero. The balance is a cached total of the ledger; the ledger is the truth.

LSP
Not every account can be debited

Fixed deposits can't be withdrawn from, so only TransactionalAccount has debit() (Chapter 30).

concurrency
Lock in a global order

Always lock the lower account ID first, with a timeout. No circular wait, no deadlock.

idempotency
Every transfer has a key

Same key → same result; the transfer runs at most once (Chapter 24).

OCP
Rules and interest are pluggable

Transfer rules form a chain; interest calculation is a strategy; alerts are observers.

Step 3 · Class diagram

Step 4 · The deadlock, and the fix

LiveTwo transfers at the same instant: A → B and B → A

Step 5 · The rest of the core code

Step 6 · Follow-up questions

Interviewer asksAnswerPrinciple / pattern
"The app runs on 10 servers. Do your Java locks still work?"No, they're per-JVM. Move atomicity into the database: one ACID transaction that locks both rows with SELECT … FOR UPDATE in ID order, or a version column for optimistic locking. At larger scale, route all operations for an account to one partition (single writer).Chapter 5, Chapter 37
"Show the statement for March."Query the ledger by account and date range; the balance column on each entry makes running balances trivial.Double-entry ledger
"Add a ₹10,000 per-transaction cap for new accounts."New NewAccountCapRule implements TransferRule; register it. Nothing else changes.OCP, Chain of Responsibility
"Transfer to another bank."The external leg is a separate system: debit locally into a suspense account, send via the payment network, then settle or reverse when the result arrives.Saga (Chapter 14), UPI (Chapter 23)
"How do you prove no money was lost?"Sum of all ledger entries must be zero; nightly reconciliation compares ledger totals with account balances and with the central bank's settlement.Invariants + reconciliation
Lock it in

Money is a value, the ledger is the truth, and locks go smallest ID first.

BigDecimal Money, double-entry ledger, LSP-safe account hierarchy, ordered locking with timeouts, idempotency keys, and rules/strategies/listeners for everything that changes.

Interview questions

What are the four conditions for deadlock, and which one does lock ordering break?

Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait (Coffman conditions). A global lock order breaks circular wait: if everyone acquires locks in the same order, a cycle can't form. tryLock with a timeout additionally breaks "wait forever".

Why store a ledger instead of just updating a balance column?

A balance alone can't explain itself. The ledger is an append-only history: it gives statements, audits, dispute resolution, and a way to rebuild or verify the balance. The balance is a cached projection of the ledger, kept in the same transaction.

Next: LLD project: multi-level IAM and auth →
40LLD · Project

LLD project: a multi-level IAM and authentication system

Identity and Access Management answers two questions on every request: who is this, and how sure are we (authentication), and what may they do on this exact resource (authorization), with permissions that flow down an organisation's hierarchy.

At Ramu's chai stall

Ramu Chai Pvt Ltd now has a finance department and an operations department, each with projects (payroll, the Kolkata branch). Ramu's rules: the owner can do anything anywhere. The finance team can view everything in finance and edit payroll. Contractors may edit operations files but may never delete anything there. And approving salary payouts needs not just a password but also the OTP on your phone; if you logged in with only a password, you're asked for the OTP right then.

"Permissions flow down the hierarchy", "a deny beats any allow", and "sensitive actions need a stronger login" are the three ideas behind AWS IAM, Google Cloud IAM and every serious enterprise access system.

Step 1 · Requirements

Authentication (multi-level)
  • Password login (level 1)
  • One-time password / TOTP (level 2)
  • Hardware security key (level 3)
  • Step-up: raise the level mid-session for sensitive actions
  • Sessions expire; lock out after repeated failures
Authorization (multi-level)
  • Resource hierarchy: organisation → department → project → resource
  • Roles bundle permissions (Viewer, Editor, Admin, PayrollApprover)
  • Bind roles to users or groups at any level; they inherit downward
  • Explicit deny policies override allows
  • Conditions (required auth level, time, network)
  • Default deny; every decision explainable and audited

Step 2 · The two halves

Step 3 · Permissions flow down the hierarchy

Step 4 · How a decision is made

  1. CollectWalk from the resource up to the root, collecting every binding whose principal is this user or one of their groups.
  2. Deny firstIf any matching deny binding grants this permission and its condition holds → DENY. Nothing can override an explicit deny.
  3. Then allowIf an allow binding grants the permission and all its conditions hold → ALLOW.
  4. Step up?If an allow would match except that the session's authentication level is too low → STEP_UP_REQUIRED (ask for OTP or a security key, then retry).
  5. Default denyNothing matched → DENY. Access must always be granted on purpose.
  6. Explain and auditReturn the reason and the trace (which binding decided), and log the decision.
LiveIAM policy playground
—

    Try: Meera deleting sales-report (explicit deny beats her Editor role); Ravi approving a payout with password only (step-up), then with OTP; Bablu writing to menu (default deny).

    Step 5 · The core model and the policy engine

    Step 6 · Making it fast and safe in production

    Cache decisions

    Cache (user, permission, resource) → decision for a short TTL, and bump a policy version on every change so caches invalidate instantly. Authorization runs on every request, so it must be cheap. (Chapter 4)

    Central engine, local enforcement

    Services call a shared policy engine (or embed a library fed with policies), and enforce at a single choke point: the API gateway or an aspect.

    Tokens carry identity, not permissions

    Put the user ID, groups and auth level in a short-lived signed token; look permissions up at check time so revoking a role takes effect quickly. (Chapter 16)

    Least privilege + audit

    Default deny, narrow roles, time-limited elevated access, and an immutable log of every decision with its reason.

    Interviewer asksAnswerPrinciple / pattern
    "Add attribute-based rules, e.g. only from the office network."Give Binding a list of Condition objects (IP range, time window, device trust); all must pass.Strategy / Specification, OCP
    "Role A should include everything role B has."Role composition: a role holds permissions plus parent roles; resolve the closure once and cache it.Composite
    "Why is Meera allowed?" from a support engineer.The Decision carries the reason and the trace; expose a policy simulator (like the playground above).Explainability
    "10 million checks per second."Decision caching, precomputed group membership, policies loaded in memory on each node, versioned invalidation via pub/sub.Chapter 4, Chapter 9
    Lock it in

    Who and how sure → what, where, and walk up the tree. Deny wins. Silence means no.

    Authentication is a chain of factors that raises a session's level; authorization collects inherited bindings, applies explicit deny → conditional allow → step-up → default deny, and explains every decision.

    Interview questions

    RBAC vs ABAC?

    Role-Based Access Control grants permissions through roles assigned to users or groups; simple to reason about and audit. Attribute-Based Access Control evaluates attributes of the user, resource, action and environment (department, owner, time, IP, MFA) against rules; more expressive but harder to audit. Most real systems use RBAC with conditions, i.e. a hybrid.

    What is step-up authentication?

    Asking an already logged-in user for a stronger factor only when they attempt a sensitive action (approve a payout, change bank details). The session's assurance level rises for a limited time. It balances security with convenience: no OTP for reading a menu, OTP for moving money.

    Why must deny override allow?

    Allows come from many places (inherited org roles, groups, project roles), so it's easy to grant something accidentally. A deny is a guardrail that must hold no matter which allow exists, e.g. "contractors may never delete in operations". If allows could override it, any new broad role would silently break the guardrail.
